subsubtopic: PAKISTAN-POSSIBILITY OF SIGNING AGREEMENT TO SELL NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY-SAFEGUARDS AGAINST BUILDING OF BOMB
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs but in his absence I shall put it to the Acting Prime Minister. In light of the statement made by the Prime Minister of Pakistan this week-end that Canada and his country were virtually at the stage of signing an agreement on nuclear exports and nuclear activity, and that the delay that has taken place so far has been on Canada's part only, until the resolution of the problem of India; now that that is behind us can the Acting Prime Minister tell the House how close we are to entering into an agreement with Pakistan?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PAKISTAN-POSSIBILITY OF SIGNING AGREEMENT TO SELL NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY-SAFEGUARDS AGAINST BUILDING OF BOMB
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot be sure about the time it will take to conclude negotiations but I can assure the hon. gentleman that we have not had the same problem in dealing with Pakistan that we had with India.

subsubtopic: PAKISTAN-POSSIBILITY OF SIGNING AGREEMENT TO SELL NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY-SAFEGUARDS AGAINST BUILDING OF BOMB
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Given the fact that the Prime Minister of Pakistan made the statement after the explosion of the Indian nuclear bomb that they were in fact looking for nuclear devices in order to balance the weapons situation between the two countries, what assurance do we have in Canada that we are not going to see a repetition of the Indian situation if we go ahead with negotiations with Pakistan? May we not find at some later date that Pakistan has built a bomb? What assurance are we going to have from the government of Pakistan before an agreement is signed that that is not going to happen?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PAKISTAN-POSSIBILITY OF SIGNING AGREEMENT TO SELL NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY-SAFEGUARDS AGAINST BUILDING OF BOMB
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. gentleman will recall the agreement we had with India said that the co-operation between Canada and India could not be used in order to enable India to produce a nuclear bomb. We had assumed from that agreement-and it turned out that our assumption was inaccurate-that it would also prohibit a nuclear explosion of any kind. In any negotiations with Pakistan, we will ensure there is no such ambiguity.

subsubtopic: PAKISTAN-POSSIBILITY OF SIGNING AGREEMENT TO SELL NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY-SAFEGUARDS AGAINST BUILDING OF BOMB
speechtext: A final supplementary, Mr. Speaker. Can the Acting Prime Minister assure the House that the terms of the safeguards agreement between Pakistan and India will be tabled in this House before that agreement is signed?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PAKISTAN-POSSIBILITY OF SIGNING AGREEMENT TO SELL NUCLEAR TECHNOLOGY-SAFEGUARDS AGAINST BUILDING OF BOMB
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I could not give that undertaking. The government takes responsibility for agreements of this kind and for all agreements with sovereign countries. This is a long standing rule that has prevailed in Canada, that the government does take responsibility for such transactions. I can assure my colleague, however, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs would have no objection after the agreement is reached, of tabling it and having whatever discussion is necessary.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SAFEGUARDS AND SANCTIONS IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR SALE TO PAKISTAN
REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SAFEGUARDS AND SANCTIONS IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR SALE TO PAKISTAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Acting Prime Minister with respect to the present negotiations with Pakistan concerning nuclear assistance. I wonder if he could give an assurance to this House that if it is not possible to table the actual agreement that the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs will make a statement on motions shortly indicating what improved inspection procedures might be in effect with respect to Pakistan? Could he also inform the House whether any sanctions will be imposed in light of the completely unacceptable situation, and apparently unworkable situation, with respect to sanctions applying to India?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SAFEGUARDS AND SANCTIONS IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR SALE TO PAKISTAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I said in answer to the previous question, in any agreement we have with Pakistan there will be no ambiguity on this point of confirming that nuclear explosions will be prohibited under the agreement.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SAFEGUARDS AND SANCTIONS IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR SALE TO PAKISTAN
speechtext: A further supplementary question. I am not sure that the Acting Prime Minister fully understood my question. I am interested to know whether in this case-as was not present in the agreement with India-there will be sanctions that will have some impact? Perhaps either he or the Prime Minister would elaborate on the question I asked the Prime Minister on May 4 with respect to some kind of collective agreement and sanctions resulting from the London Club agreement. I believe the Prime Minister at that time offered to give me that kind of indication or assurance, so that we might know that negotiations with Pakistan would provide real protection.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SAFEGUARDS AND SANCTIONS IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR SALE TO PAKISTAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will take that request under consideration and discuss it with the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I return to my previous answer to the hon. member's question. In the case of India, the problem was that India claimed that it had not broken the agreement it made with Canada and therefore that it had not in any way merited the kinds of sanctions we found it necessary to employ by way of withholding aid for certain purposes and denying further nuclear co-operation. That arose because India would not agree with our interpretation of the agreement. Therefore, on this occasion, we will try to enter into an agreement with Pakistan, if one emerges, an agreement which avoids the ambiguities which led to the difficulties with India.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Considering the finding of the C.D. Howe Research Institute that data used during the past many months for comparing United States and Canadian levels of productivity increases was in serious error, that instead of Canadian productivity increases being half that of U.S. for the period 1969-74 Canadian productivity increases were twice as great as the United States, would the minister confirm that the government itself based a number of its recent major economic decisions on that erroneous data?

ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM ALLEGATION WRONG DATA USED AS BASIS FOR IMPOSITION OF PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is some understatement. We have gone from a claim to being only half as productive to being twice as productive in terms of increases. That's some difference. As the minister, when introducing the wage and price control program last fall, said that cost-push inflation threatened to price our goods out of world markets, will he now admit that his data then was wrong and that it was the major justification for a wage and price control program? If that is so, if he has now changed his mind, as he just acknowledged in his answer and admitted that the data was wrong, does the program have any further justification?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM ALLEGATION WRONG DATA USED AS BASIS FOR IMPOSITION OF PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had occasion last fall and many times since, both inside and outside the House, to point out that until the middle of the summer of 1975 we could not justly blame wage settlements in Canada as being the basis for the creation of inflation in Canada. As we pointed out in introducing the anti-inflation program, we were concerned because in the fall of 1975 the level of demands in wage negotiations and, indeed, wage settlements themselves, running up to between 20 per cent and 30 per cent had created, in the words of the hon. gentleman, a threat which would put the Canadian economy, in time, in a disadvanta-

geous position. We were faced with the threat of a substantial cost addition to the Canadian economy which would affect our competitive position. As I pointed out many times, for that reason we introduced the program not because of figures existing prior to the middle of 1975.

speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. For the first time in five years Canadian wage increases were running ahead of United States wage increases for a number of months, and the minister says the government had to bring in a program to deal with that. We do not agree. The minister said more recently that 50 per cent of the goods we produce is intended for export. I point out that only 28 per cent of the manufacturing sector in Canada is in the export business, or primarily in the export business. Considering this correction of his own recent figures, will he now reconsider the government's position announced in the budget on the issue of the tax cut and bring forward a tax cut soon for the average and low income people as the principal means of stimulating the Canadian economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF TAX CUTS FOR AVERAGE AND LOW-INCOME GROUPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the first assertion made by the hon. member, indeed it had to be of concern to a great many Canadians, if not to the hon. member and his colleagues, that the rate of inflation last October was 10.6 per cent. Simply the fact that there had been this move in the wage rates in Canada had to be of serious consideration. The fact was that a 10.6 per cent rate of inflation was more than we felt Canadians should bear. The hon. member has never given any indication as to what, if anything, he would have done about the increase.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of National Defence, I will direct my question to his parliamentary secretary. He has been given notice of the question. Has the United States been testing or are they going to test their new sleeping torpedo, sometimes called the Captor, at the underwater test station at Nanoose Bay?

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice A. Dionne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: TESTING OF NEW UNITED STATES TORPEDO AT NANOOSE BAY-FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENTS FOR USE OF TEST STATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of the question. The delivery system of the Captor is indeed being tested at Nanoose range. I might point out that the Captor carries a charge of approximately one pound.

subsubtopic: TESTING OF NEW UNITED STATES TORPEDO AT NANOOSE BAY-FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENTS FOR USE OF TEST STATION
speechtext:
One pound is about all that a nuclear warhead weighs. Can the parliamentary secretary advise

the House as to the financial arrangements between Canada and the United States for the use of the Nanoose installation? We carry out so little in the way of weapon development ourselves that I imagine it is used mainly by the Americans. Can the parliamentary secretary tell us just what are the financial arrangements between the two countries with respect to the use of this station?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: TESTING OF NEW UNITED STATES TORPEDO AT NANOOSE BAY-FINANCIAL ARRANGEMENTS FOR USE OF TEST STATION
speechtext:
The
Nanoose range is an acoustic range for testing underwater devices; its facilities are shared between the Americans and ourselves. We supply the range itself and half the personnel, while the Americans supply the test equipment and the other half of the personnel. There is a sharing of information. The range is used for underwater testing because the water there is relatively quiet and deep and because it is one of the few sites available on the West Coast for such a purpose. It is not unusual for Canada to share the range with other nations. As a matter of fact, not too long ago the Russians, with Canadian concurrence, used the range for testing the Pisces.

LEVEL OF POLYCHLORINATED BIPHENYLS IN GREAT LAKES- REASON FOR DELAY IN GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: My question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the fact that polychlorinated biphenyls have been found in the Great Lakes to be eight times higher than the permitted level of two parts per million, with the result that all fish now caught in the Great Lakes are highly contaminated and people eating these fish also become contaminated with a deleterious and toxic substance that is both cumulative and remains in the body indefinitely, I should like to ask the minister what immediate steps he is contemplating to counteract this serious human health problem?

subtopic: LEVEL OF POLYCHLORINATED BIPHENYLS IN GREAT LAKES- REASON FOR DELAY IN GOVERNMENT ACTION

In re-examining all that was said at that time, I have come to the conclusion that no question of disorder exists with respect to the reply made by the minister on Friday. Business of the House
member for Fundy-Royal further questions may be put to either or both ministers involved.

For that purpose, we have deliberately decided not to proceed with certain items on the order paper at this session, and we have proposed an extension of hours of sitting so that the remaining urgent business can be disposed of without an undesirable curtailment of debate. The items which remain on the urgent list are the following: Bill C-68, which is now at third reading; Bill C-81, which is now at report stage; Bill C-84, which is now being debated at second reading; Bill C-87, debate on which has not yet begun; Bill C-88, which is now at report stage; and Bill S-35, which is now before a standing committee.
These six items, all except one of which has already been the subject of extensive debate, plus the budget resolutions and supply, constitute the government's program before adjournment. Unless some emergency arises, the government has no other items which it considers essential to be disposed of before the adjournment. The parties may, of course, be ready to agree on the approval of minor housekeeping matters such as motions Nos. 33 and 34 under government business.
Let me add a word or two about Bill C-83, which is now before the standing committee. It is desirable that progress be made in dealing with this piece of legislation, and the government will be proposing amendments resulting from public representations which will, we hope, be helpful in ensuring its approval. The government, however, will not keep the House in session for the purpose of advancing this bill. If the standing committee has not reported by the time of adjournment, it may of course decide to sit during the recess. I shall be discussing with the other parties an agreement to take up the bill in the new session at the stage which is reached at the time of prorogation of the present session. To be as precise as I can be, the government will propose the adjournment of the House when the six items to which I have referred, plus the budget resolutions and supply, have been disposed of, whether that happens before or after June 30, except for the usual

provision by which Mr. Speaker could call the House back for royal assent.
Mr. Speaker, seventy speakers have taken part in the debate on Bill C-84. I am informed that there is still a long list of speakers who wish to be heard. I have proposed to the House leaders an extension of hours for the purpose of that debate only, two additional hours in the mornings on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the temporary suspension of private members' hour.
May I also remind those who may be concerned about the timing of the vote on second reading that the House has already approved an order which avoids a quick, unexpected vote. The timing of the vote will be decided by the House leaders within a week after the end of the debate, so that those who are absent from Ottawa can get here for the occasion.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS OF FINKELMAN REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just over three years ago the chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, Mr. Jacob Finkel-man, was asked by the government:
-to examine the Public Service Staff Relations Act and its administration and to make recommendations, having regard to the experience gained since that act came into force, as to how it should be amended or revised in order to meet adequately the needs of the employer and the employees in the public service and the employee organizations that represent them, and to serve the interest of the public.
This undertaking was given the full support of both government and opposition parties of this House, as well as that of the employee associations of the public service. The confidence in Mr. Finkelman which was expressed at that time was demonstrated to have been well placed when, about a year later, the results of his exhaustive study were tabled. I think it is a tribute to Mr. Finkelman, who is now coming to the end of his distinguished public service career, that this confidence should have been expressed in such a concrete way.

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS OF FINKELMAN REPORT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS OF FINKELMAN REPORT
speechtext:
In recognition of the importance of the questions raised in Mr. Finkelman's report and of the many far-reaching recommendations which he made-I recall they totalled some 230 specific recommendations-the report was given very careful examination by the Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service. The joint committee involved a variety of interested parties in its deliberations, including-and I quote from its report:
Bargaining agents representing employees in the public service of Canada: unions representing views outside the public service of Canada: the Treasury Board secretariat representing the government as employer; employer groups in the private sector; the chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board and the chairman of the Public Service Commission; personnel and labour relations specialists; university professors; and interested individuals.	.
Mr. Speaker, I am aware that many people, and particularly some of those who, through interest or vocation, are closely associated with public service employer-employee relations matters, have from time to time expressed impatience at the length of time the review of the legislation covering collective bargaining in the federal public service has taken. I have shared this concern. I can only say, however, Mr. Speaker, that it is better to take the time if that time is necessary to ensure that the action proposed is the wisest and best course to follow.
The joint committee issued its report in February of this year, and since that time the government has been actively
Public Service
studying its conclusions and its recommendations, as well as going over again those proposals of Mr. Finkelman which were not touched on in the committee's report. All of this work is being conducted in light of the extensive hearings of the committee and of the many discussions which have been held informally over the past several years between government officials and representatives of the interested parties. The issues are extremely complex and the factors and considerations which must be taken account of are numerous, interacting, frequently subtle, and sometimes conflicting. In view of the time already spent in laying the foundation for definitive proposals to be put to the House by the government, I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that members would not want the government to table prematurely, hastily prepared and inadequately considered legislation.
In any case, the legislative calendar for the session we are now engaged in is already very full. We have heard some protests on the six items that I thought constituted very limited scope for the rest of the session. You will not disagree with me I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that we are in a rather congested state as far as the rest of the session is concerned. The government intends, therefore, to complete its internal deliberations relating to public service collective bargaining as quickly as possible, and to introduce legislation in the next session of parliament which, hopefully, will begin in the fall.
With regard to the Public Service Employment Act, the joint committee recommended that the Public Service Commission, after consultation with the bargaining agents and the employer, develop proposals for early revision of the act and that a task force be set up to undertake a longer term and more fundamental review of the role of the commission. The consultations relating to early revisions have been completed and the commission's proposals are now being considered by the government. The related amendments to the Public Service Employment Act will be introduced in the next session, probably at the same time as new legislation covering the Public Service Staff Relations Act.
Mr. Speaker, the government will also, as part of its ongoing examination of government management and organization, be looking into the more fundamental and far-reaching questions which prompted the joint committee's recommendations for a special task force to study the role of the Public Service Commission in relation to employer-employee relations matters. The government is sympathetic to the concerns which underlie these questions and will ensure that they are examined.
Initially, an interagency task force including representatives from the Privy Council office, the Public Service Commission, the Public Service Staff Relations Board, the Treasury Board secretariat, and the Department of Labour is being set up with terms of reference authorizing it to examine the principles and practices relating to appointment, staffing and training in the public service and to make recommendations for changes calculated to serve the interests of the public, to contribute to the over-all improvement of the public service and to foster good employer-employee relations. Such a task force will obviously need to consult extensively with all interested bodies, with special emphasis on the many and varied

May 31, 1976
Public Service
employee associations. I trust that the task force will undertake its work as expeditiously as possible, and barring unforeseen difficulties that the government will be able to report on its results during the next session of parliament.

subsubtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS OF FINKELMAN REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with tradition, I wish to thank the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) for supplying us with a copy of his statement in advance-by 20 minutes-of this sitting. Having read the report, I wonder why it was not possible to give it to us last Friday so that we could have looked it over, or why it was not given to us today and the statement made tomorrow.
Aside from that rather mild admonition, speaking on behalf of this party I should like to say that we welcome this long-awaited declaration, even while we confess to some dismay that it contains little more than another indication of governmental delay. At least now we have some sort of timetable, if only in the form of a promissory note. The government has produced a timetable, and that is about all. It intends to proceed in accordance with the priorities of its own program. That is about all the statement says.
At the beginning of his statement, the President of the Privy Council stated specifically that three years ago the government had asked the chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board to review present legislation on public service staff relations and its administration, with a view to making recommendations on how to improve the public service generally to better meet public interests.
That was over three years ago, Mr. Speaker, and we have just learned, with the excuses to which we have become accustomed, that for the time being the government does not want to formulate final proposals in that regard. [English]
Three years ago the government asked for an examination of this question and for recommendations. On November 13, 1974, a joint committee of this House and the other place met to study the proposals put forward by the chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board. That examination was carried out most fully. On behalf of my party, may I associate myself with the high words of commendation describing the work performed by the chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, Mr. Finkelman.
After innumerable meetings and after hearing the evidence of interested parties, the special joint committee produced a detailed report of its findings and made recommendations relating to a variety of employer-employee relations aspects in the public service, including such matters as the right to strike, managerial exclusions, designated personnel, the entire bargaining process, and so on. In February of this year the report was tabled. It included 72 recommendations or resolutions.
The government all along was aware of the proceedings of the special joint committee and could have formulated detailed guidelines to cover each of the important sectors being considered by the committee. I suggest that at the

very least the government should now have brought forward a series of broad proposals outlining the areas with which the legislation will deal when it comes forward. It would not have been necessary to put these proposals in legislative form, but they could have outlined areas with which the legislation would deal and explained omissions in the legislation of areas covered by the committee. For example, each of the 72 recommendations could have been reviewed, and in an appropriate space opposite each recommendation the government could have said, "Yes, we will accept this," or "No, we will not accept this", or "We will look into this particular matter", or "We find that it will be impossible to change this particular matter."
As matters now stand, we have nothing but another promise to consider, a not unusual performance. If the kind of broad propositions to which I have alluded had been put forward, we might have had the opportunity during the summer to elicit reactions of interested parties. Without doubt, the government will expect us to rush the legislation through whenever it chooses to bring it before the House. I assure the government, and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp), that my party considers the proposed legislation so important and so serious that it does not intend to be rushed in its deliberations, but looks forward to fair and extensive consultation.

The special committee has also made recommendations on legislation governing employment in the public service, and in particular the part the commission must play. According to the government, final proposals with regard to that aspect of the report will also be postponed; we hope, for our part, that they will not be put off indefinitely. We are therefore awaiting with some impatience the two bills to be introduced by the government in this regard. Those two bills, once introduced, should enable us to solve the many problems posed by present legislation.

speechtext:
On this side of the House planting is more difficult than it is on the other side. The statement says that the government has studied the report; it noted that the committee wants revisions made in the Public Service Staff Relations Act, that it wants a study made of the Public Service Employment Act, and that it wants the appointment of a task force. The minister now says, "We are making the first study, but we have not yet got the new bill. We hope to have it in the fall. We are carrying out the second suggestion and have had a study made of the Public Service Employment Act, but are not yet ready to introduce a bill. As for the proposed task force, one is being set up, and in the fall we hope to have a report." I do not know why the minister employed the device of the ministerial statement to put so little before the House. Perhaps he wanted to indulge in the following choice comment when he said:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that members would not want the government to table prematurely hastily prepared and inadequately considered legislation.
You know, that sort of thing happens so often around here that I am surprised the minister would bother to say that. I suppose, as the hon. member who spoke on behalf of the Conservative party said, we now at least have a kind of timetable, a promissory note for legislation in the fall. The minister did not say which fall; I presume he meant the fall of 1976.
Sir, having said that the statement is hardly worth all this fuss, I had better be brief, and I shall be. I warn the minister and the government that the adoption of the report by the special joint committee was not unanimous. Some of us feel strongly that suggestions in the report give the government too much of a green light to go too far in terms of imposing excessive fines on union members and unions, in terms of other restrictions, enlarging the areas of designation, enlarging managerial exclusions, and so on. If the government is really concerned about good employer-employee relations, I urge it to look at the good things in the report but to beware of some of the pitfalls in it.
In the latter part of his statement, the minister said that one of the aims of the government is to foster good employer-employee relations. May I draw one item to his attention, after which I shall conclude. The matter has come to rest in the Privy Council office. I refer to a document called a "Personal history form" which many public servants are called upon to complete as part of a security check. It is being used widely in the Department of National Revenue and in other departments as well. The form has all the earmarks of a witch-hunt. One of the questions public servants are asked to answer is, "Where was your mother-in-law born?" What possible connection can that have with a public servant's right to a promotion?
I mention this today because I have been working on it, without bringing it to the floor of the House, for a couple of years. I have been in correspondence with the former chairman of the Public Service Commission. However, only recently I was told that matters have bogged down and that I had better write to an official in the Privy Council office. I did so and received a courteous reply from the official. But the writer of that reply could not tell me when something would be done about this, despite the
Public Service
many protests. I give the minister that assignment to work on since it is now in the Privy Council office. If he wants to have good employer-employee relations, he should not be asking public service employees, before they can get certain promotions, the birth place of one's mother-in law.
I said that we need to take much time on this, so I better not take any more. I am glad we shall get some action in the fall. I hope it will be the fall of 1976, and I hope the government will pay attention to some of the comments being made today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is rather surprising to note that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) stated in the House today that the government is prepared to introduce measures or make recommendations about its relations with the civil service as early as next autumn.
Mr. Speaker, the President of the Privy Council has just said to the House that more than three years ago the government gave to Public Service Staff Relations Board Chairman Jacob Finkelman a mandate to study the relations between the federal government and the civil service. Now, the minister says that a year later the chairman did report the results of his thorough study. This means that for over two years the government has been well acquainted with the recommendations of that committee appointed by the government to consider relations between the government and the civil service.
It is hoped the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) will keep his promise and bring forward next fall legislation or recommendations in the field of relations between the public service and government. One thing I wish is that we would not see on the federal level the mess we are seeing in Quebec in the relations between the public service, that is the public and quasi-public employees and the government. There has been friction for too many years already at the expense of the taxpayer who must pay for both sides, for both the employees and the employer, because it must be owned that the federal government today is the employer who levies the highest taxes in Canada, the most labour intensive industry. The same can be said for the provincial level in Quebec as well as in Ontario.
Yet we hear those public servants yelling: "Higher pay, higher pay!". They do not realize that they are not paid from the profits of a business, but from the taxes of Canadians.
When they yell rightly or wrongly: "Higher pay!", they should display at the same time cards which read: "We want more and higher taxes, so as to get higher wages". I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that we will not see that here in Canada from the government, the unions nor the public service. Let us hope that as soon as the parliamentary business will resume, the government will bring forward specific legislation to foster understanding and cooperation between the public service and itself.

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, May 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last ten years hon. members of this House have had to give their opinion on capital punishment and to take part in four important debates on this subject.
On October 24, 1973, the Parliament of Canada decided for the abolition of the death penalty by 119 votes against 106, except for the murder of security guards, prison guards and policemen. On that occasion, Mr. Speaker, I voted for Bill C-2.
Today, I would like to enumerate the reasons why I changed my views and I shall describe the process of the consultation I had to undertake.
I for one attach great value to the general attitude we have toward life, the dignity of the human being and the character of people and that prompts me to act prudently while deciding whether the state should intervene in the life or death of a human being. If we refuse to the state the right to take the life of one of its members, we should, to be consistent, deny it the right to deprive someone of freedom for his lifetime and to remove all hope of freedom.
Is it not just as cruel to imprison a human being for 25 years without any rehabilitation opportunity as prescribed by Bill C-84 now before the House? First, I wish to explain the different categories of murders and see if capital punishment has a deterrent effect or not and what are the possibilities of hanging an innocent victim. As I said earlier, we must first place the debate in its actual context and define the procedure concerning the identification of the presumed offender or define the categories of murders punishable by death.

May 31, 1976

But we should not think that the retentionists are potential jailers and that they would be ready to apply capital punishment for all murders. I am favorable to rehabilitation policies and during my experience in Parliament I dealt with some cases and I have two examples of persons who have been rehabilitated in the riding I have the honour to represent and I can say that I believe in rehabilitation as those two people are now well adapted and very active in society and are not parasites living off society. On the other hand, I love life too much to let those who have no respect for the life of others walk freely in the streets.
So, I wish to clearly classify murders in two categories as prescribed by the legislation that makes a distinction between first degree murder, that is a planned and deliberate murder including contracted murder, the murder of a policeman or a prison or penitentiary employee acting in the course of their duties. First degree murder is also the murder committed during the highjacking of an aircraft, a kidnapping or some sexual offense including rape and attempted rape. Those are first degree murders. Second degree murder includes all other murders including crime due to jealousy. The definition of first degree and second degree murders should be well understood.
What are the new penalties applied under Bill C-84 now under study? A person convicted of first degree murder will be sentenced to 25 years' imprisonment before being eligible for parole for the first time.
A person convicted of second degree murder may be eligible for parole only after 10 full years in prison. However, the judge may, if the jury so recommends, extend to 25 years the mandatory prison sentence without parole.
So, there are the differences between the two categories of murders and the penalties provided for in Bill C-84.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to answer some of the questions we may ask ourselves or make a few comments about some of the statements made by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) when he launched the debate on this bill on May 3 last, when he said that those who believe in the deterrent value of the death penalty are maybe a little more simplistic, a little more narrow-minded. I do not want to report him as saying things he did not say, that is why I would like to remind him of his statement as recorded on page 13089 of Hansard.
I also heard some members take a stand against the death penalty because they think is has no deterrent effect and, here again, we are provided with statistical data. The solicitor General said that those who claim that the increase in the number of murders is due to the fact that there has not been any execution in Canada since 1962 are wrong and mislead those who listen to them.
I will refrain from quoting a whole part of the speech because my time is limited, but in any case I respect the view expressed by the Solicitor General, although I do not agree with the terms he used, and I also respect my colleagues who expressed the same view. But I have a lot of reservations before using this argument in favour of the abolition of the death penalty. Those figures do not single out the deterrent effect because they were not established with a view to drawing conclusions, but with a view to
Capital Punishment
confirming a conclusion which was already made through a moral and philosophic reasoning or else, by intuition.
Statistical data give rise to various interpretations. It is almost impossible to make useful comparisons between various countries because of the differences in the legal definition, in crimes, in the practices of the various departments concerned, in the different courts, in the way of gathering criminal data which differ from one country to another, in the morality and behaviour standards and finally in the political, economic and social conditions of those various countries.
I believe, however, that we can quite naturally assume that the professional criminal who views prison as a trade hazard considers the death penalty as something quite different. Clearly, when a murder is committed, there has been no deterrent. But this in no way implies capital punishment did not deter other inmates from committing murder. Statistics are impossible to obtain on that possibility, on the number of people who did not commit murder. Offences only are reported. Those cases where the offence was not committed appear nowhere in statistics. It seems to me that on the basis of statistics only, it cannot be stated that capital punishment is not a deterrent, because it is said that since it was abolished, there does not appear to be a rising crime rate.
Even referring to the research centre report entitled: A study of capital punishment as evidenced by Canadian associations, which was published by the Solicitor General and which very clearly refers to the criminal behaviour trend from 1962 to 1970, while in 1962, the rate was 1.7 per
100,000	people 7 years old or more, the rate was 2.3 in 1970. Looking at statistics of attempted murders appearing in the same report in Table 33, we see that the rate went from 0.5 per 100,000 in 1962 to 1.4 in 1970. Therefore, the rate is on the increase. I believe there is always a danger in comparing statistics from different countries with and without capital punishment. This is always subject to errors.
My decision was taken in the light of information received, a document I consulted, and also my personal experience. I would like to stress to the hon. members that there is actually a deterrence, although some would argue to the contrary. I am referring to hangings at the Bordeaux prison, in the north end of Montreal. On the evenings where somebody was hanged, people used to gather in front of the prison. There was complete silence among those people. Everyone waited for the flag to be hoisted, confirming that the poor victim was dead.
I went there twice and I admit that I did not remain indifferent. One cannot remain insensitive to such a spectacle, if I may call it that. We were all silent and sad and in favour of mercy on the part of the jury or the Supreme Court. As to the inmates inside the prisons, a chaplain confirmed to me that it was a day of mourning for all of them, and that the mourning did not last only one day but several days before and after the hanging. The inmates really refected and realized that this penalty given for a crime, I am still talking of premeditated murder, gave a true idea of the horror it inspires to most people.
That day certainly included for inmates and members of criminal circles outside, that is members of the mafia or organized crime, moments of refection which, in my esti-

May 31, 1976
Capital Punishment
mation, were and are likely to prevent other crimes by the inmates who are spending jail terms of 25 years such as proposed in the bill and will at least act as a deterrent for the inmates. Prisoners are not motivated in any way toward good conduct because they are in for 25 years. What will they loose by committing a second murder? For them, there is no possibility of rehabilitation. Following this process, Mr. Speaker, I for one believe that capital punishment acts as a deterrent.
Secondly, what is the danger or risk of making a mistake and hanging an innocent victim? It seems to me that the development of social legislation and gratuities, and the advantages of legal assistance for court defence and of identification of the true victims by medical procedures, by the unanimous decision of the jury, the Appeals Court and the Supreme Court eliminate all possibility of error during the trial. And speaking about unanimity of the jury, I would like to refer to the trial of Jean-Guy Dubois and Jacques Ouimet, where the ninth member of the jury had some doubts and the judge asked for a new trial. This trial will take place in the fall. I believe that this is certainly a precaution which aims at preventing innocent people from becoming victims of the death penalty.
In my opinion, the present situation is much more dangerous to the extent that innocents are victimized without a trial. If we continue the present system, that is if we maintain the abolition of the death penalty, and even if we eliminate the exceptions that I mentioned at the beginning of my speech, if we completely abolish the death penalty, I believe that such an attitude will greatly increase the danger that innocent people would become the victims, and without benefit of a trial.
I am very concerned that simply to defend themselves, people will shoot to stop the first criminal attempt. For instance, you will recall the pharmacist who saw someone go into his store and simply to defend himself, chose to shoot first instead of becoming a victim. It seems to me that the present situation is more dangerous, that is that Canadian citizens run a greater risk of being innocent victims now than if the death penalty were established within the framework that I mentioned at the beginning of my speech.
As concerns social defence theoreticians who blame society for everything, it seems to me that they have a tendency to negate individual responsibility. It is true that we have established all sorts of services or social and even protectionist policies, and I have always been in favour of such initiatives, which form the basis of civilization, of love, of friendship, and I would even say of human society. But for some people, the establishment of these structures becomes a means to evade their responsibities.
For some, all these programs constitute a way to evade their responsibilities, and they rely only on others and prefer letting the community do everything instead of developing a personal interest or motivation for work, and a discipline for life. If they have a problem, they prefer to dilute their responsibility on the rest of the community.
Generalization of that belief leads to the conclusion that society alone is responsible for the mistakes of individuals. I think a criminogenic virus more powerful in itself than all its pharmacopoeia and likely to ruin its action is being maintained and fed. Capital punishment should not be 
considered as pure vengeance, nor those who are in favour of capital punishment as more simplistic minds than others. It is healthy for society to be able to condemn symbolically a sordid crime. To deny society that right would be to urge it to show more severity for crime and downgrade its standards of public morality.
In concluding I will support all rehabilitation measures for inmates who accept to live within society. And I hope to have the opportunity at other times to speak on the measures I would like to see implemented in the area of rehabilitation, measures that I already advocated at the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary before, unfortunately, a decision was made to wind up in three stages all farm production material on that 400 acre farm where vegetables, meat and dairy products were produced on the farm, and an unfortunate decision was made to close that farm altogether and buy at retail prices all the food required for the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary and the Archambault Institute. I think in that context we could have got a rehabilitation policy going.
So I suggest that the courts make it a priority to proceed with the trial of an alleged murderer and that deliberation take place in a reasonable delay rather than cases being postponed for two or three years. Quite often witnesses could not be found; I am not talking about a very short delay so that public opinion, feeling and emotion can be aroused through the papers, but a reasonable delay. I think we should make it a priority to hear those trials, and in a reasonable delay. Mr. Speaker, if Parliament votes the abolition of capital punishment I ask the government to amend the law so at least a second time murderer will be subject to capital punishment, and that his trial be proceeded with as soon as possible.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to follow my good friend, the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Roy), and I congratulate him on a well reasoned and well thought-out speech. As the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) indicated today, this has been a very long debate, with in the order of 70 speakers participating so far. This reflects the great importance members place on this issue and the deep sense of conviction members hold on both sides of the question. Because of this, they feel compelled to speak and place on record their views and, indeed, the views of their constituents.
As other speakers who have preceded me have indicated, this is certainly not one of the most pleasurable debates in which one might participate. There have been a number of speeches covering, in essence, every aspect of this important subject. There have been excellent presentations on both sides of the issue. I have listened to a great number of those speeches and have read many more, and regardless of the view one might hold on this subject, one cannot be anything but impressed by the very high calibre and sincerity hon. members have displayed in their approach to the issue.
I do not wish to minimize the contribution of any member who has taken part in the debate, and certainly not of the hon. member who preceded me for whom I have
May 31, 1976

developed a great amount of respect and admiration over the years. But I must say, after reading the speeches, I was most impressed by the contribution of such members as the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Masniuk), the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche), the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik), the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) and, on Friday, the very thoughtful presentation by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). To those hon. members who did not have an opportunity of hearing those speeches or have not as yet had an opportunity of reading them, I would certainly commend them for reading.
There is no question but that the issue of capital punishment has once again caused widespread concern and further active debate in all parts of Canada. As one hon. member has put it in this House, there is a feeling of anxiety and quiet desperation toward the whole issue of violent crime in our society and the manner with which this government in particular has approached it. The anxiety, quite frankly, involves the safety and security of all citizens in Canada. There is growing apprehension as to what will be done, if anything, to restore safety and security in Canada.
Most of us have received a great deal of mail on this subject, and some of us have conducted surveys. Some of the comments we have heard from our constituents can be summed up by phrases such as: murderers should be treated as a threat to society and not as a menace to society; either keep them in prison and a long way from society, or definitely reinstate the death penalty. Perhaps their feelings can be summed up by a phrase of this order: we do not need murderers walking around to murder again, or the expense of keeping them in jail. There is a general feeling of desperation and frustration. I can assure the House that the feeling of concern is widespread and most genuine.
Through this bill we are once again asked to place our positions on the line. A vote for this bill will, in fact, be a vote to abolish capital punishment and a vote against will be a vote to reconfirm the five-year partial abolition which expires, I believe, in 1978. The first question which arises in my mind is why we have to be dealing with this piece of legislation at this particular time. This law still has another 2'A years or so to run. We have a law on the statute books and it is amazing to me that we find ourselves dealing with this particular issue at a time when we have so many other important issues facing the country. One can only assume that this is an attempt to divert attention from the real issues facing the country, or an attempt to divert our attention from getting at the root causes of violent crime. For whatever reason, the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and the government have seen fit to bring this bill forward, we as members are called upon again to render another decision.
Most members will agree that this is not a clearcut issue. Nor is it easy to rationalize or decide which is the best route to choose in casting one's vote on this issue. It is perhaps the most agonizing deliberation I have ever engaged in, and I am sure it is agonizing to all hon. members, at least judging from the sincerity and the
Capital Punishment
manner in which hon. members have made their individual presentations to the House. The issue is associated with religious, philosophical and traditional connotations. It is related, as well, to such factors and considerations as rehabilitation, the question and philosophy of punishment, the philosophy of revenge and reform, and whether or not capital punishment is a deterrent to murder. There have been convincing arguments on both sides of the issue.
Moreover, we have been bombarded by reams of statistical data as well as the historical evaluation and study of capital punishment-courtesy of the Solicitor General's department! We have been subjected to a fair amount of so-called expert opinion, if you will, from those who conveniently endorse the Solicitor General's view. Quite frankly, I really must question the objective validity of some of those so-called expert opinions placed before us. Those people, in my view, have an obvious bias, as does anyone who participates in this debate, and in my view they simply set out to rationalize or justify their views by applying selected statistics, and interpreting those statistics to the best advantage in support of their viewpoints.
I suppose that is fair and part of debate, or part of putting forward one's own particular point of view, but I say that this circumstance should be made abundantly clear. Quite frankly, I question whether in fact there are any real experts in this particular field. If so, who are they, because, as the hon. member for Laval just pointed out, you can manipulate statistics to prove any point of view- and we see it happening in this case. We see statistical evidence used to support either point of view quite effectively.
So I believe that one has to rely upon one's own beliefs and whatever view one has, supported by his evidence and supported by one's constituents-if you will, one's own gut feeling. If the bill should pass, it will in effect give approval to the past actions of the government, since the law which we now have on the books has not been implemented. In my view, the government has failed to enforce the spirit and the intent of the law. Yet I am aware of the fact that the governor in council may commute a sentence of death to imprisonment for life or invoke the royal prerogative of mercy, but I wonder whether, by applying those two sections in every case, the real intent and spirit of the law is complied with. I submit it is not. What is irritating Canadians more than anything else is simply the failure of the government to comply with the spirit of our laws. In that connection, I circulated a survey to my constituents in response to which I received some comments which appeared on the form from a resident in the Vegreville federal constituency. The comments read:
Can we be certain after the last legislation in which, when police and prison guards were murdered and their murderers were supposed to get the death penalty and didn't, that this new legislation is going to help the situation? If that was not enforced, how can we be certain that this will be? Will these murderers be out on the streets again in a year or two, or will we finally stand behind our legislation? In the way in which our legislation is getting more lenient, in a few years will murder be legalized?
I think that sums up the irritation and the frustration of many Canadians across this land. To a large number of Canadians this government has simply flaunted the law. I
13988

government on the basis of who gets the most votes and in turn the most seats. I believe that to ignore public opinion on this issue is inconsistent and contemptuous of majority rule. That is an affront to one of the basic principles of democracy. After all, governments get elected by a majority, which is an expression of a majority opinion. For those who might disagree with my rationale, I suggest that we choose a national referendum to settle the subject once and for all.
I say once again that there is a growing amount of cynicism about politics, politicians and our democratic institutions. Much of this emanates from the failure of our politicians accurately to reflect the views of those whom they represent. I believe in democracy. The issue before us is indeed difficult and complex, and I believe that when we are faced with an issue as sensitive as this, one which goes to the very core of our social and moral fabric, we should solve it, not by ignoring the wishes of the majority of Canadians but by accepting the wishes of the majority. Very clearly, the majority of Canadians are opposed to total abolition. That is the position of the majority of my constituents, and that is the position I shall take when I cast my vote on this bill.

Mr. Speaker, this debate on this occasion, under the circumstances of the economic ills facing this country, seems to me to be put a red herring designed strictly to captivate public attention and to turn aside from those matters which the government should really be addressing itself to rather than this. First, there was Bill C-83, an omnibus bill designed, one would almost say, to be sure that people would be taken away from the problems of wage and price controls, the problems of unemployment and many other important problems. Then to top it off, along comes Bill C-84.
Bill C-84 marks the fifth time in my career in this House that there has been debate on capital punishment. In 1958 there was a motion by the then member for Scarborough, Frank McGee. There was no vote on that occasion. Then is 1966 or thereabouts there was a government motion, a resolution which did not carry. It was defeated. Then in 1967, in a quick volte face, the government came forward with a bill restricting capital punishment. This was repeated in 1972 with the five-year renewal, and now we are faced with the total abolition of capital punishment. Considering what the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski) and other hon. members in this House have said, and public opinion being what it is, one wonders at the sanity and the purpose of the government in bringing forward this matter at this time.

Very well, Mr. Speaker. The reason I raise this point is that I am not always too sure the speech is the view of the hon. member who is making it. I also find it a bad practice to have a copy of the speech and to hand it to the media. The media have access to the "blues", the working copies, and can get their reports quickly. There is no need for a written copy to be handed to the media.
Interest in capital punishment has waxed and waned. No capital sentence has been carried out since 1962, despite clearcut indications that the exercise of the royal prerogative by the cabinet has been nothing short of blatant abuse. In 1964-65 we had the Santa Claus murder case, and there was a sort of five minutes to midnight commutation. There had been no recommendation for mercy in this cold-blooded killing of policemen and yet there was a commutation.
There was another instance where I know hon. members on the other side were violently aroused by the crime, one of the most violent Canada has seen, when one, Dionne, raped and murdered four children in Quebec City. His sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. What for? He was subsequently killed in prison by other inmates.
Mr. Speaker, I want to make the point that I feel the sentence of whole life imprisonment is a cold, sadistic act. We read of the Roman dictators who are reported to have given slaves the right to life; they were turned loose in a pit of lions unarmed, and if they could kill the lions their lives were preserved. It is the same sort of thing today to put into the prison system a man who has been found guilty of murder, particularly certain types of murder. He is going to be killed. Pontius Pilate could not have been more cynical. The government claims that he has not been sentenced to death, that his sentence has been commuted to 25 years or 15 years; but the human wolves in the penal system will get him, Mr. Speaker. As sure as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) are drawing breath today, those men will die.
What do we do with a "Williams"? What do we do with that unfortunate individual in Saskatoon who killed those four children? Do we put them into the penal system because they have a right to their lives? That is the argument made to justify the abolition of capital punishment, that the state has not the right to take a life. But, Mr. Speaker, the individual who is put into the penal system will be killed. That makes it that much more sadistic on the part of legislators who say that for those humane and moral reasons they are going to abolish capital punishment. Instead of the hangman's noose, it is knife or it is strangling. Instead of the hangman's noose, are we to see beatings to death in prison? Does anyone think that alter-
May 31, 1976

ing the form of punishment will make society feel better? Does anyone think that we are wrapping a mantle of self-righteousness about ourselves if we decree the abolition of existing forms of capital punishment, yet send men and women to a much crueller, more sadistic death? What we are being asked to do makes a travesty of our system of justice.
I think the 1967 restrictions were the result of an abandonment of so-called moral principles which provided for the abolition of capital punishment. Before 1967 we heard about those moral principles; we have not heard much about them in this debate. One can cite Scripture any way one chooses. It is almost like statistics. Scripture can be used to justify almost any case. Surely to goodness, what is law if it is not the formal expression-

I will table the hon. member, too.
For the benefit of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain, I say that law is the formal expression of a rule of conduct of a human society, for the benefit and protection of that society, which is accepted by that society. Why is the government proposing the change to the Criminal Code, in the guise of Bill C-84, a change which Canadian society does not want to accept? Either I am right or all our mail, surveys and polls, are wrong. Canadian society does not want to accept the abolition of capital punishment, does not accept the punishment for murder as contained in Bill C-84, life imprisonment only, and has shown that it is concerned about its own protection. The law shall be for the protection of society. If the law protects adequately, why, as the hon. member for Vegreville asked some moments ago, is there the present preoccupation, in the public mind, with protection? The reason is that the law is failing to protect the public. Certainly, there is a great deal more violence these days; but the law should protect the public from violence, and it does not.
By introducing a bill providing for partial abolition, the government of 1967 threw a sop to its backbenchers who wanted to protect prison guards and policemen. The principle of that bill involved limited protection; of course, immediately the bill became law, that principle went out the window. Without doubt, the 1967 bill was based on arguments of so-called higher moral values. In order to get Bill C-2 through the House, the government had to agree on two categories of capital offences, capital murder and non-capital murder. Once those categories were established and the bill passed, the cabinet went through what I consider a most cynical exercise. I think between 1967 and 1972 it really went to the point of misleading parliament as it had no intention at all of having capital sentences carried out. Despite all the protection given in the courts, it was never intended to carry out a capital sentence.
Capital Punishment
Now we are considering Bill C-84. The reason, I suggest, is that there is a backlog, a waiting line of men who have been found guilty of capital murder within the restrictions of the present law. By having the present bill passed, the cabinet hopes to avoid the responsibilities of the law which it brought forward in 1972. I do not like Bill C-84. I do not believe in the abolition of the death penalty, and never have. Since 1958, in every debate on capital punishment in which I participated I have been against the abolition of the death penalty. I favour the law which was introduced in 1961 and in force until 1967, a law providing for the division into capital and non-capital categories of that heinous crime, murder.
I anticipated that this year there might be a debate on capital punishment and therefore conducted a survey in 1975, which continued from September until November. I sent out 47,000 questionnaires to homes in Edmonton West, and received about 7,300 returns, or 15 per cent. Incidentally, the returns were carefully analysed as to the sex of the person replying, age group, whether male or female, and marital status. I sent a copy of the results of the questionnaire to every member of the cabinet. I must tell hon. members that several cabinet ministers privately indicated to me that when they see results like these it shows how sadly out of touch they are with public opinion. Let me read the first question on the questionnaire, and the result: Capital punishment (death by hanging) is presently limited to those convicted of murdering an on-duty police officer or prison guard, and conviction can be commuted to life imprisonment by the cabinet. Are you in favour of:
(a)	retention of the law as it now stands?
"Yes", 2 per cent.
In other words, 150 out of 7,300 answered that they were satisfied with the retention of the law as it now stands. I continue:
(b)	retention of the present law with the addition of severe limits on the rights of commutation?
"Yes", 6 per cent.
(c)	any sentence of life imprisonment for capital murder being with (8 per cent-605) or without (50 per cent-3,681) provisions for parole?
In other words, that is a sentence to life imprisonment and throw away the key.
(d)	having the death penalty applicable to anyone convicted of premeditated murder, murder for personal gain, or murder resulting from a crime of violence such as armed robbery, rape, etc., without distinction as to the victim?
"Yes", 76 per cent.
(e)	the total abolition of capital punishment?
"Yes", 9 per cent.
That is what the people of my constituency think about the subject of abolition of capital punishment. There was a further return on a question asked by the Edmonton Police Association. The question read:
I believe in extending the sentence of capital punishment to all premeditated murder and murder committed during the commission of a crime. Yes or no.
I received 1,700 copies of this newspaper clipping which is very simplistic in its terms. Of those, 89 per cent replied yes, they were in favour of the extension of capital punishment for all premeditated murder and murder committed

during the commission of a crime. Many years ago there was a royal commission on capital punishment in the United Kingdom, 1949-1953.1 quote from that report:
We think it is reasonable to suppose that the deterrent force of capital punishment operates not only by affecting the conscious thoughts of individuals tempted to commit murder, but also by building up in the community, over a long period of time, a deep feeling of peculiar abhorrence for the crime of murder. "The fact that men are hung for murder is one great reason why murder is considered so dreadful a crime."
Murder is a dreadful crime. We use a very awesome and dread-producing penalty. It has been said by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and many others that capital punishment has not been a deterrent to murder because murder is still committed. Capital punishment is not a 100 per cent solution to preventing murder. There is no punishment that is a 100 per cent deterrent or preventer of crime. I suppose one might say that capital punishment is right because the person who is executed will not commit any crimes thereafter, but that is the only sure one.
I find it passing strange that in all this argument, abolitionists say to those who would retain capital punishment "prove your case". Why? After all, is it not up to those who advocate a change to prove their case? It is the abolitionists who wish to change the law. Let them prove their case. Do not ask those who would retain capital punishment to prove their case. The onus is on those who wish to make the change. That is a principle of law and it will always apply.
In so far as deterrence is concerned, there are no statistics with regard to why a person was deterred. If I asked the hon. member who is just leaving the chamber whether he had ever been deterred from committing crime, since he did not commit a crime, he would not come forward to say so. No one who has been deterred from committing a crime will come forward and say that they were prepared to shoot or knife an individual, but because of capital punishment they did not do it. Therefore, the question of statistics is a totally bogus argument. In the report of the royal commission on capital punishment in the United Kingdom, Lord Justice Denning, as he then was, said:
The punishment inflicted for grave crimes should adequately reflect the revulsion felt by the great majority of citizens for them. It is a mistake to consider the objects of punishment as being deterrent or reformative or preventive and nothing else.. . The ultimate justification of any punishment is not that it is a deterrent, but that it is the emphatic denunciation by the community of a crime: and from this point of view, there are some murders which, in the present state of public opinion, demand the most emphatic denunciation of all, namely the death penalty.

The House resumed from Monday, December 9, 1974, the motion of Mr. Clark:
That, in the opinion of this House, a committee should be selected to consider the powers, prerogatives and privileges attaching to the office of Prime Minister and to report what safeguards are desirable or necessary to secure the constitutional principles of the sovereignty of parliament and the supremacy of the law.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED COMMITTEE STUDY OF POWERS, PREROGATIVES AND PRIVILEGES OF OFFICE OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am indebted to the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Blais) for underscoring the change in status of the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark), as he then was-a change in status which I feel confident will be changed even further as a result of the next foray in our political system before the electors of this country. I think it important that all members of parliament, backbenchers, cabinet ministers-yes, even the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-should read and reread the speech of the hon. member for Rocky Mountain, now Leader of the Opposition, which was delivered in this House on December 9, 1974, when the motion before us was introduced in his name.
There are a number of reasons why the office of the Prime Minister should be subject to scrutiny by all of us as we look ahead as representatives of the people of this country. First is the increasing ease with which all of us, particularly the Prime Minister, are able to communicate with the public. Then there is the effect of the changes in the rules of the House, which has been to emphasize the pre-eminent position of the government and, in particular, of the office of the Prime Minister.
I do not propose to reread the speech delivered by the Leader of the Opposition in 1974, but I do think it is well worth quoting from his remarks as recorded at page 2071 of Hansard. Speaking briefly about the office of the Prime Minister, he had this to say:
The Prime Minister comes to the question period on most days, but the questions are usually about his judgment, seldom about his powers; and anyway there is no requirement that he answer. After the so-called Pearson precedent of 1968 there is a real question whether parliament can defeat a Prime Minister by vote in this House except on matters of obvious confidence, like a budget. If our capacity to defeat a Prime Minister is so limited, so is our capacity limited to control him by the
May 31, 1976

threat of defeat. As the chief minister, he is less bound by Treasury Board than any of his colleagues, and appointments to or by his office can be made without recourse to the Public Service Commission. His estimates are brought before the miscellaneous estimates committee. However, they are not dealt with there by him, but by a parliamentary secretary to another minister.
The Prime Minister reports to no standing committee and there is no statute to define his responsibilities. Ironically, parliament probably has less real control over the Prime Minister than we have over the president of Air Canada or the president of CNR, because a Crown corporation is established by statute while the Prime Minister's office is not, and its officials must appear regularly before standing committees while the Prime Minister's officials do not. No matter how loosely you define "responsible" government, parliament should have some direct control over the actions of its Prime Minister beyond his mere appearance for questions in the House. If that has been important in the past, I suggest it will be even more critical in the future, for reasons I will enumerate.
I believe the phrases I have read lay the groundwork for the consideration of the motion before us. There were four main points which the Leader of the Opposition brought out on that day, and I believe he did so most eloquently. Initiative, under our parliamentary system, lies with the cabinet. The conduct of public business and accountability for public business rests with the cabinet. Government itself is growing and, as a consequence, the powers of the Prime Minister appear to be growing to a corresponding degree.
The reform of our Standing Orders in 1969, and the way in which the revised rules have been used since that time both in this chamber and in the committees, have made it clear that the effect was to remove from backbenchers on both sides the right to scrutinize and, where necessary, to delay. In other words, the cabinet is no longer the servant of the House but the House has become the handmaiden of cabinet. This is particularly the case when there is a majority government, but the situation is notable even in a minority situation where one might think the effect would be minimal.
Consider the way in which access to television has affected the role of the Prime Minister. The House will recall that recently, on the occasion when the right hon. gentleman changed his mind and turned his back on what he had said earlier with regard to price controls, he spoke outside the House of Commons, away from the ministry, making the announcement directly over television. Other members of the cabinet have used television in similar circumstances. Notable, recently, was the way in which the budget was handled in terms of the dissemination of information to the public. The Prime Minister has access to television by virtue of his office. He has shown an ability to use this medium in a way which affects the operations of the House and in a manner beyond the capacity of any other member of the House, including those who sit with him around the cabinet table.
Then, again, the point was made that the Prime Minister really has a department of his own. That is exactly what the Privy Council office has become. It is a department whose power is contained only within limits set by the Prime Minister himself. It operates in the complete absence of scrutiny by parliament. This, in itself, makes the establishment of a committee of investigation, such as is proposed in the motion, an urgent matter. Comments have been made in the House from time to time concerning the right of the Prime Minister to control, through his
Prime Minister's Office
office, access to television. My hon. friend from Halifax, the former leader of the official opposition has a bill on the order paper calling for the establishment of procedures which will permit other party leaders to have similar access to the media.
If the result of the imposition of television upon the parliamentary process is the one we have seen so far, then surely it is only fair that the Leader of the Opposition and other party leaders should have a similar right. I mentioned the Leader of the Opposition in particular because according to our precedents he is the leader of the alternative government. I hope I shall not be hurting the feelings of hon. members opposite if I say that backbench MPs on the government side are, under our system, largely dependent upon the personality and style of the Prime Minister for their influence, and that if MPs are, in the words of the Prime Minister, nobodies, then he has made them so as a result of the way in which he has used his office and the power in his hands. He is really the first among equals, as was traditionally the case. He has no equal when it comes to status within our parliamentary system.
Improvements in House procedures in the direction of greater accessibility to information would help government backbenchers as well as members of the opposition. If government backbenchers were able to take advantage of these improved procedures, perhaps they would have more credibility as critics than they have today, and the Prime Minister might be forced to listen to them. The fact of the matter is that, unlike the operation of the parliament of Westminster, backbenchers opposite sit mute and do not criticize the Prime Minister. I would ask any of my colleagues who have witnessed the House at Westminster in operation to compare the questions that are asked by government backbenchers of their own ministers with the kind of planted questions and the floating of questions that seem to characterize the operations of this House.
