subsubtopic: SUGGESTED COMMITTEE STUDY OF POWERS, PREROGATIVES AND PRIVILEGES OF OFFICE OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to leave the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) under the impression that I waited after his speech to speak, because I intended to do so in any event.
Mr. Speaker, it is fortunate that the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) gave us by his motion the opportunity to reassess an important aspect of the Canadian government process, in this instance the office of the right hon. Prime Minister.
Indeed, that very process underwent profound changes in the last fifteen years and it is vital to recognize the critical development of its growth and emphasize its underlying patterns, particularly in the light of the harsh criticisms arising there from.
Public administration in Canada is a very vast area of which political power is but a part, the legislative power being one of the two main components, that is Parliament on the one hand and the executive power on the other.
Prime Minister's Office
With this debate on the office of the Prime Minister and its prerogatives it is the whole matter of the responsibility of the executive before the House of Commons and consequently the means made available to the elected representatives to exercise effectively and intelligently that very control that is being questioned. There is talk about it periodically, and the matter itself is not new.
However, none of the hon. members who spoke before me it seems has yet explained the very operation of the office of the Prime Minister nor brought to light its structure and components. In fact, the office of the Prime Minister is not a new concept, its present size and influence being the main source of the many criticisms, sometimes warranted, most often unwarranted, voiced by elected representatives in the last few years out of spite, impatience or frustation.
It is not my intention here to open the file of the lack of information available to parliamentarians, nor to criticize the procedure used in our deliberations. May I simply say that there is a deep feeling of uneasiness which is reflected by the impatience directed towards the executive and its head.
To explain the enlarged staff of the Prime Minister's office, one must understand once again that for about ten years the whole governmental system has been suffering from an acute crisis of gigantism which results from a change in the philosophy on the role of the state and from a serious questioning of the Keynesian neo-classical theory of economic mechanisms.
In short, let us simply point out that it is now obvious that the market is no longer self-regulating and that for the survival of our institutions and of our standard of living, it is now essential, even at the risk of being branded as interventionists, that the state take a more active part, sometimes very bluntly and aggressively, through monetary, fiscal or socialistic policies, to put private interests in line with those of the whole collectivity, and thus prevent the resource redistribution, dear to the defenders of the so-called classical economy, from becoming a lure.
Yet this increased interference resulted in the creation of new governmental or quasi-governmental organizations first aimed at informing the government on the tendencies and economic indicators and acting as a consultative body for the development of the necessary policies and regulations. On the other hand, within the departments, new orientations were developed when it was not whole new departments as those of Regional Economic Expansion, Manpower, Housing and Environment. So, we have seen the staff of the public service grow considerably to meet those new responsibilities and those new spheres of activity.
The Prime Minister is by definition-I should say by tradition-the one who must coordinate the legislative and executive activities of the government system and as such, he must stay in continuing communication with the departments through his ministers, with the provinces through the officials of the division of federal-provincial relationship, with Parliament through the House of Commons and last, with the public through information media.
13996

May 31, 1976
Prime Minister's Office
It is a fact that the size and the influence of the Prime Minister's office have considerably increased since the accession to power of the present Prime Minister. I shall comment later the main effects of that boulimia but, first, it is important to understand that rather than to establish a parallel structure it was necessary to keep contact or try to keep contact and consequently to control the main structure. But to some extent, and at the risk of making unfounded statements, I shall say that the Prime Minister's office succeded better in that respect than ourselves the members of Parliament.
For some time, the public service has been accused of being tentacular, self-sufficient and syndromatically uncontrollable. I agree with that to some extent but I think there are good motives for its original impulsion as I said earlier and that practical considerations made it inflate itself like the frog in Lafontaine's fables.
In principle, it is Parliament's function to make sure that the public service is operating adequately. In practice, in the present circumstances and with the available means, the only person in a position to hold it back, on occasion, is the Prime Minister-through his influence more than through his real powers. Therefore, by necessity, the office of the Prime Minister has become a service organization having as a secondary but indispensable and important function an advisory function. There is every reason to applaud at this new trend: when one considers our inefficiency, that of the legislative, one must be glad that someone is controlling the monster the public service has become.
The motion of the hon. leader of the opposition asks that we set up a special committee to examine the role and influence of the office of the Prime Minister with regard to Parliament's right to scrutinize and criticize the executive. In fact, the extent of the powers, I should say the influence of the office of the Prime Minister is already known. That influence results from the necessities of daily life, from those of the changing public administration, from the Prime Minister himself assuming the powers of control and supervision over the government machinery, powers which he already had under the Constitution, but had never been exercised to their full extent. In short, it does not stem so much from the preparation of a putsch, as has often been suggested, but rather from the daily necessities of administration. My concerns are not, a priori, in respect of that, for the executive must administer, and so much the better if it finds the tools to do so.
But where does Parliament come into the picture? Is the House of Commons really losing some of its influence, some of its powers? And at a higher level, could we go so far as to say that at this time of exponential acceleration of changes in values and accepted ideas, the British parliamentary system, which can be described as traditional and rigorous, is no longer capable of adapting to new conditions to meet effectively the needs of a modern state? This is indeed where the question lies. Does our system still answer our needs today, as it is, and has always been, without change, without major adjustment, without a will to progress?
The Prime Minister is still responsible before his elected peers, the cabinet is still collectively accountable before the legislative body, but are we, as parliamentarians, in a

position to make a judgement on the activities of the executive that would be well-informed and exact? My answer is no. Without trying to analyse the rights and wrongs of our system, which has certainly rendered great services in the past, and has even demonstrated on occasion an extraordinary versatility, and has even been the guardian of democracy which we all cherish, our dear good old system has grown old and will have to undergo a serious lifting to show a new and acceptable look.
Instead of studying the prerogatives of the Prime Minister's office, we should rather take a look at ourselves, make a serious self-examination. To me, the very principle of ministerial responsibility is partly gone because it deprives the House of Commons of the very power it is supposed to wield, the sanction of the legislative or administrative measures taken by the executive. Except in some extraordinary circumstance, or in case of some never-heard-of crisis, government members will very unlikely take the risk of bringing the government down, except, as I said, in case of some essential question, or if the representatives, for serious personal reasons, cannot approve the position of their party, as expressed by the bills introduced by the cabinet, and which bind them, as they bind in their favour the government members, and as they bind the opposition members.
The party line is a gaping wound in and otherwise healthy body and I am surprised that few people have not seriously questioned it yet or have not proposed its mere abolition. There should only subsist, occasionally and in very special circumstances, what is usually called non-confidence votes, whereas all the members should interest themselves in the existence of the government and be able to judge in conditions similar to those that prevail today in all divisions. Abandoning the party line would give more value to the primary function we are supposed to hold in system of government, that of a law-making body, a role which has been disguised and which does not mean a word in the present situation. We should underline that, according to the fact, it is no longer sure that, since the precedent of 1967, the government can be brought down otherwise than with a non-confidence vote, but the threat still remains and prevents the members from acting according to their own conscience. Parliament has become a moral sanction for the actions of a small group, a moral sanction which abides by the necessity of politics and not by judgement and reason. This same little group is the instrument of a bigger administrative system, an arrogant and self-satisfied machinery.
I do not necessarily advocate some republican system as in the United States where the president freely choses his ministers and advisors without taking into account the contingencies of an election, although it would however be very fortunate, at times, to have the necessary flexibility so that the Prime Minister could bring into his cabinet a non-elected person, some authority in a particular area, when this authority is not available "on the bench". The present sacrosanct principle of ministerial responsibility is fiercely against it, but by substituting to it another type of real responsibilities through votes of non confidence against the Prime Minister, such impediment is thus removed as well as the attendant sclerosis.

The decision which must or will have to be taken one day or another will be whether the legislation is really a public responsibility or that of the government which approves it through a minister who introduces it as the consequence of a partisan policy but not a necessarily valid one of the party in power whose members are bound by a context of penalties and rewards, the carrot and stick, but this is much more serious by the fear of suddenly plunging the country in the confusion of some general election. The opposition should not rejoice too loudly, because it is the victim of the same restraints, but in the opposite way and cannot have a good laugh at this deplorable situation.
I foresee the day when all members of this House-and that applies as well as to the opposition members as to the government members-may be able without fear of reprisals and especially without fear of harmful effects for the state's stability, to decide in all conscience of the intrinsic value of bills brought in through the executive or otherwise. Either we are idiots without any professional conscience, any competence, real idiots then! If we continue to act as puppets, I see absolutely no use for this institution, except to save appearances and to constitue a feed tank for ambition. Either we change the spirit that is prevailing here but not only the spirit but the game's rule as well, then we will see appear the very reason for our being here, for what we are fighting for relentlessly: democracy. We will represent the people and we will act as adults and responsible people.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, in principle-and until I am given proof to the contrary, which has not been done yet- I have as much confidence in the 264 elected representatives now present, in their efficiency and their sense of duty, as in the administration where anonymity prevails and which does not have to give any account to anyone, in spite of appearances, because we must always save appearances.

He says that the question period is no good for his purposes, and I am sure that the cabinet ministers would agree.
This Chamber, quite frankly, is a rather unworkable entity in 1976. The hon. gentleman's motion attempts to aggravate an already overworked system of parliamentary procedure which should be swept into the ash can of history.

In our protective and isolated manner we refuse to appoint outside experts to suggest a new role for this Chamber, as has been done under the British system.
The hon. member for Rocky Mountain asks for a regimented, structured procedure to examine the actions of the Prime Minister. He did not suggest anywhere in his address opening this debate that parliament is already bogged down.
It is my contention that this parliament examines the role, the powers, and the actions of the Prime Minister as completely as any parliament in the world. Because of the freedom exercised by the Chair during question period- which I am not questioning-hon. members of the opposition have a field day. That is good. It is good to have the opportunity every day for ten months of the year to grill the Prime Minister. Any member can ask questions, any number of questions is allowed, and questioners have a chance to become overnight heroes if they have done their homework, or overnight national flops if they have not.
There is a duty incumbent not only on the government side but also on the opposition side to keep things in perspective. The hon. member for Rocky Mountain, in a roundabout way, alluded to this. There are energies and money being expended in this Chamber and it is important to keep things in perspective. Canada is not just Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver; Canada is Canada, and Canada's problems are many and diverse. It is important always to keep that in mind.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time I should like to make a joint announcement with my colleague, the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, concerning the government's domestic feed grain policy.
In May, 1974, we outlined a new domestic feed grain policy. The main objective of that policy is to encourage the growth of livestock and feed grain production across the country according to the natural potential of each region, and to have a fair pricing system for all Canadian feed grains.
This is still our objective. But we are making modifications to the policy in order to make it work more effectively. As some hon. members know, we have experienced some problems in domestic feed grain pricing during the past year. We want to avoid similar problems in the future. For that reason we are taking action to assure that domestic feed grains are available at corn-competitive prices. We are relocating part of our reserve stocks. We are changing rates of feed freight assistance to some parts of the country. And we are using some of the funds we had been putting into feed freight assistance to set up new programs to assist feed and livestock producers.
These new developments in our domestic feed grain policy will guarantee a dependable flow of western feed grain to the domestic market at competitive prices. They should also relieve any temporary shortages and disparities in regional markets. Our actions will benefit both eastern and western farmers. I know that eastern Canadian livestock producers will be pleased to have their feed grain supplies made more secure. And we are protecting the domestic feed grain market for our Canadian producers by ensuring that prices stay competitive with United States corn.
The minister responsible for the Wheat Board will explain what actions the Canadian Wheat Board will be taking to keep prices corn-competitive. I would like to fill in a few details for you on the other points.
Modifications in feed freight assistance rates will go into effect on August 1 of this year. In British Columbia the rates will be reduced by $4 per ton. In Ontario and western Quebec all rates of assistance of $6 per ton and less will be eliminated. Other rates in these areas will be adjusted accordingly.
Most of the rates in eastern Quebec and the rates in the Maritimes will not be changed. Livestock producers in these areas have a greater reliance on outside supplies of feed grains. Feed freight assistance will also be available- (Mr. Speaker.]
I repeat, will also be available-on shipments of Ontario corn and wheat to the maritimes and eastern Quebec.
Because western grains are going to be available at corn-competitive prices I do not expect the reduction in feed freight assistance to increase feed grain prices in eastern Canada or British Columbia. Imported corn has and will continue to set the ceiling on feed grain prices in Canada.
We have informed the provincial agriculture departments in Quebec, Ontario, and British Columbia about these policy developments. And we have discussed with them setting up adjustment programs in areas where feed freight assistance has been reduced. During the next five years we will use the funds released from feed freight assistance to develop the feed and livestock industries in these provinces. To date we have not determined the actual locations and amounts for the re-allocation of domestic feed grain reserve stocks, but the Reserve Stock Management Committee will be moving stocks closer to feed grain deficient areas of the country.
If temporary regional or national shortages of feed grains are identified in the future by the Canadian Livestock Feed Board and the Canadian Wheat Board, import permits will be made available by the Wheat Board.
As a final check that our domestic feed grain policy is doing its job I will be monitoring the domestic feed grain market through the Canadian Livestock Feed Board. If there is evidence of bad pricing or supply practices in the market place, the Canadian Livestock Feed Board will be permitted to intervene directly in the market place should intervention be required to eliminate such practices.

With the announcement today of the partial change in feed grains assistance there is an accompanying indication by the Canadian Wheat Board that from August 1, 1976, it will be offering western feed grains to the domestic market at prices competitive with United States corn. The Canadian Wheat Board will offer grain at a daily flat base at Thunder Bay and western country elevator points. Prices at these points will be the Montreal corn-competitive price less transportation and handling costs.
The actual timing and technical nature of the change to this pricing structure between now and August 1 will be established through consultation between the Canadian Livestock Feed Board and the Canadian Wheat Board.
The opportunity for prairie producers to make direct non-board sales of western feed grains will continue. Board offers to the domestic market will help keep the market corn-competitive and preserve it for domestic grain producers.
As the Minister of Agriculture has indicated, we will be arranging the move forward closer to feed-grain deficient areas of the major portions of the reserve stock of feed

grains which was set up following the 1974 announcement with these arrangements, with feed grain available at corn-competitive prices, and with direct purchases from producers available when that is the desirable option, we have every optimism that the supply of feed grain in feed grain deficient areas will be cared for.
However, in order to reassure temporary situations, as the Minister of Agriculture has said, import permits will be made available by the Canadian Wheat Board when the Canadian Livestock Feed Board and the Canadian Wheat Board identify the need in that particular situation. As I heard the two ministers talking I wondered whether the left hand does not trust the right hand when it gets behind the back. This certainly indicates to the people of Canada that agriculture is a divided industry and that the Government of Canada does not know whose responsibility it actually is. They want to play it safe.
I was rather confused and somewhat concerned as I read the statement of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). It should be recognized as classic "Whelanese" at its best. It had to be drawn from the lessons taught by Mackenzie King, so that he could say something which meant everything to everybody and nothing to anybody, and he could say anything he liked thereafter and agree with what he said earlier.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: That is the greatest compliment you have ever paid me.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
This is going to be the decision of the Minister of Agriculture. It certainly leaves agriculture in a dilemma. They are not sure which way they are going nor from whence they have come after such a dialogue.
There is a very important aspect of this in so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned. The recognition of the imperative requirement of the livestock industry of the Atlantic area by the revision of the feed grain subsidies is something which the Atlantic area feared might be overlooked by the Government of Canada to some degree. That has been left in place. I would be remiss in my duty if I did not point out that there has been no recognition of the erosion of the effectiveness of the feed-grain subsidy as it applies to the Atlantic area. May I give two quick examples.
When the initial concept of feed-grain subsidies was brought into place the disparity of cost in grains east of the Great Lakes was 50 cents per ton as you went from station to station throughout eastern Canada. That disparity has increased because the feed-grain subsidy has been frozen at its specific level. It has not taken up the increases in freight rates which have been added year after year.
The disparity in prices now at various points in eastern Canada on grains is $10 per ton. In the mill-feed sector, and this is an important requirement of the industry, the disparity in price from Thunder Bay to the extremities of eastern Canada is as much as $35 per ton. Therefore the value has eroded to a very large extent.
It has reached the point in the Atlantic area where the livestock and meat producing industry find that cost-wise in respect of production they are barely competitive with meats shipped from western Canada, particularly the Winnipeg area. They have been asking for an improvement in the structure by recognizing the increments in cost that are contained in the cost of other ingredients in the feed industry such as minerals, vitamins, and protein concentrates. To date this has not been recognized.
We ask that one of the two ministers give this consideration, whichever is responsible, and we are not quite sure who it is at this time. I ask that minister to take a cost

May 31, 1976
Feed Grains
benefit and see just where the Atlantic provinces meat industry stands with regard to competition with other sectors of Canada. Has the grain subsidy in fact attained the objective for which it was intended, namely, to make the cost of meat production in the Atlantic area competitive with supplies from other areas of Canada?
At no time has Atlantic Canada asked that meat be produced there more cheaply than in other areas of Canada. However, it has asked that the subsidy allow it to be produced as cheaply there as in other areas of Canada and delivered to our markets. After all, we are a meat deficient area and we would like to encourage that industry.
I am concerned about that area of Canada from which this subsidy has been removed completely. As I understand it, any subsidy of less than $6 per ton will be gone as of August 1. Where does this leave the feeder in eastern Ontario and western Quebec? They are far from the sources of corn which is supposed to be the substitute for western grain as far as possible. They do have onerous freight charges to bear. They are in competition with other areas which are closer to feed sources. I believe the ministers should jointly reconsider this question. I note the minister's statement that he has discussed this statement with Ontario and Quebec, but he does not give us any indication of what those provinces said in reply to his proposals or what the effect is likely to be on the livestock-poultry industry in Eastern Ontario and Western Quebec vis-a-vis other areas of Canada.
I am puzzled about this nebulous something-or-other upon which the savings are to be spent by way of promoting the livestock industry in Ontario, Quebec, and British Columbia. The words are, as I understand it-"The savings shall be used for the development of the industry in those provinces." There are a multitude of ways in which this money might be used. It might be used, for example, to construct grain storage facilities at strategic points. But the phrase "development of" or "improvement of" applicable to the industry in those provinces is, indeed, nebulous.
What will be the effect on British Colombia? This is a subject on which I am not an expert. However, I submit that having regard to the support which the industry in that province has been receiving from its provincial government it can ill afford grain which will be more expensive than the grain it has been feeding to date. The statement contains no suggestions to the contrary, so perhaps the government of British Columbia can afford to chip in a little more.
The location of the reserves referred to in these statements is important. What is even more important is that these reserves of grain be available on demand to the feeder. In the past it has been government policy to place grain in position and in reserve. If an eastern feeder anywhere in eastern Canada required a car of grain which was not available it could be drawn from stocks at a particular point, but it had to be replaced by the buyer. This program was not usable in the main by eastern feeders because the replacement cost was under the control of the Wheat Board. It was not a case of drawing a car from

Prescott and having it replaced in Thunder Bay or even at Prescott; it was a case of withdrawing a car from a point of reserve and paying the price determined by the Wheat Board for its replacement. Is there any cure for this? Will the minister, through the Canadian Livestock Feed Board, be able to eliminate the cost of drawing from reserves in particular locations? The seller should be able to negotiate with the Wheat Board directly at no cost for withdrawal from reserves.
Will Wheat Board permits be available on call in emergency, or only after cutting through a great deal of red tape? I realize that the minister's remarks were very brief. Perhaps had they been longer and more detailed it would have been easier to make a short reply. But the indirect and oblique approach taken to this subject makes it difficult to reply except by asking questions and being somewhat critical.
There is one notable omission from this statement. During the election campaign of 1974 the Minister of Transport, or the minister responsible for the Wheat Board-I am not sure in which capacity he has spoken tonight-promised there would be a recognition of the inequities which exist in the meat industry of western Canada with respect to transportation costs. Every agriculturalist in Canada was expecting that this statement tonight by the associated ministers would cover that item. The undertaking was initially denied, but on January 28, 1975, if my memory serves me correctly, in response to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) it was acknowledged that this had been an election promise and the undertaking was made, and that a statement would be forthcoming in the future. A year and several months have passed since that date. A statement has been made and this aspect has not been touched upon. The trading policies of the government have treated the industry in a cavalier manner. Trade with the United States has been difficult. We have put up artificial barriers which have been countered with further artificial barriers.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Order. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member but the time used by the two ministers combined was about seven minutes. The hon. member has already been speaking for ten minutes and if he were allowed to continue a few minutes longer he would double their time. Bearing in mind, also, that we are to hear two other speakers on the same subject I should have to ask him to conclude briefly.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I respect your ruling, Mr. Speaker, and will sum up shortly. We are tinkering with a very important industry-the grain industry and the feed industry. We are not being specific. We are not being direct except in certain respects, and for some of those things we are grateful. But there are some areas which will suffer and others which will benefit. There are aspects to which greater attention must be paid. I would ask the two hon. gentlemen who have made statements to keep in mind the requirements which still exist. A total policy should now be brought forward, one which would result in complete equity for the grain and meat business in Canada.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was hoping that when the minister in charge of the Wheat Board rose tonight he would at least have had the
May 31, 1976

grace to blush. With this announcement he is admitting through the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) that his feed grain policy of May, 1974, is a total failure.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Nonsense!

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
The Canadian Wheat Board has always been ready to maintain access of western barley and other feed grains into the eastern market. It has been to the advantage of western grain producers to stay in the eastern market. But now, if I read the statement correctly, feed grain prices to western grain producers are to be reduced by the amount of reduction in feed freight assistance. In effect the announcement means lower incomes for western grain producers. That would be bad enough, but with these lower returns to feed grain producers there are no guarantees of any kind for the producers.
The minister has been horsing around for two years and now he has turned full circle. He is back in the court of the Canadian Wheat Board. The Board will be required to offer feed grains at prices competitive with those of U.S. corn and feed grain, and I would like to know what effect that will have on the bargaining position of the Board. If they have an export market available at 20, 30 or 40 cents a bushel more for barley, the Board's capacity to sell will be limited by the amount they are required to hold in reserve to maintain prices competitive with U.S. corn. That in turn will mean either lower feed grain prices on export markets for some portion of the Wheat Board's product, or it could mean lower export sales because we are holding back bushels at U.S. government competitive prices. If the Wheat Board is subject to the Livestock Feed Board the board will also have to supply the prairie market and the B.C. market with feed grains.
I should like an explanation either from the Minister of Agriculture or the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board as to how much, if any, U.S. corn moves into British Columbia, and what relationship there is between the barley price and the U.S. corn price in British Columbia, or in southern Alberta for that matter. I suggest there is none whatsoever. Any feeder is entitled to call on the Canadian Wheat Board for corn at competitive prices, which usually means lower prices for western Canadian grain.
The minister in charge of the Wheat Board has fooled around with feed grains on the open market and on the commodity exchange for the last two years. Since he is putting the Wheat Board in this position he has to admit that the open market for feed grains has been a total failure. My question to the minister, which if he does not answer soon I hope he will answer later, is this: why do we need an open market and commodity exchange in light of the joint announcement of himself and the Minister of Agriculture?
It seems to me that the eastern feed grains market takes whatever it requires from local markets on the prairies, and British Columbia now takes priority for what is required over the export market. The Canadian Wheat Board is required to hold and maintain its stocks.
Let me make another point. What is meant by the relocation of these reserves? Is the Canadian Wheat Board now
Feed Grains
going to be required to hold stocks in Halifax, St. John's, Montreal, Prescott, and Port Colborne, at U.S. corn prices? We would like to know. In a short year for U.S. corn the Canadian Wheat Board must provide buffer stocks. If that is the case, when are the Minister of Agriculture and the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board going to get rid of the commodity market, since it is obviously not working? The western grain producers are being made responsible for feed grain supplies. What now about a guaranteed price for feed grains? If the Wheat Board is going to be required to guarantee reserve stocks which will be relocated somewhere, what about a guaranteed price? According to these two ministers they are now subject to the whims of the U.S. corn market, which I submit will be of no benefit to the consumers of meat and of very little benefit to the feeders in the Atlantic provinces, Quebec, Ontario, and British Columbia.
I am also wondering what are the government's plans regarding the eight cent per bushel tariff on U.S. corn that is presently in existence. Will the government give that up? If so, what will it get in return? If the Minister of Agriculture does look a little paunchy I wish he would not start reaching for Santa Claus clothes. I think it is a mistake to require the Canadian Wheat Board to hold reserves. If they are the marketing agency, then let them market. They have responsibility for marketing, so let the Canadian Wheat Board do the marketing in all of Canada.
In conclusion, we feel that what we really need is a Canadian grains board that is the governing body over grains from the Pacific to the Atlantic ocean. Prices, from the producer of feed grains to the consumer of feed grains, should be negotiated and agreed upon as between one end of the country and the other. We do not need a commodities exchange and open market. In fact a Canadian grains board, as and when we cannot meet our own needs for barley, oats and other feed grains, would do the purchasing of U.S. corn at the best possible price. The cost of feed grain would be pooled among the users of feed grain. Yet these people opposite have the imagination of a door knob; they keep clinging to nineteenth century concepts even when these concepts have not worked for two years.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board has been fooling around with feed grains on the open market, but he has not retreated. He did not say so tonight; he had the Minister of Agriculture get up and say it for him. This concept has not worked and it will not work. We should like to have a lot more detailed explanation about this from the minister in the days to come.
We want to know what is meant by the relocation of reserve stocks. We want to know what effect this will have on feed prices to western grain producers under the feed freight assistance rates. We would like to know what are the government's intentions as to the involvement of the so-called open and free market now that the Canadian Wheat Board has been delegated additional responsibilities that have nothing to do with marketing but with reserve stocks at U.S. corn-competitive prices. We will be interested in hearing from the government on those points.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture a question. Does this statement mean that finally we will get some

May 31, 1976
Feed Grains
assistance to provide the long awaited additional terminal facilities for the storage of corn in southwestern Ontario, close to the minister's home area, or shall I have to ask the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board whether he would allow that?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope an announcement will be made shortly regarding the grain storage program that has been talked about for several months. I am sure the hon. member knows there is more interest in that area than just a grain storage depot; there is a whole agricultural complex to be developed in that great part of southwestern Ontario.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am wondering whether the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board will state whether or not there will be any compulsion to sell grain from the Wheat Board. Are they going to be forced to compete with the market, or will they have a choice?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the statement indicates, I have reported the agreement of the Canadian Wheat Board to sell on this basis. They are therefore prepared to give the assurance, so there is no doubt about it, that there will be daily flat pricing of barley and other feed grains for the domestic market at Thunder Bay on a basis equivalent to bringing the grain to Montreal at corn-competitive prices.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The minister did not answer my question. If they see fit to sell this grain at some other place and corn is available in the United States, will they be forced to put the grain on the market at competitive prices, or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The corn-competitive offering really means that it will be close enough to the corn price, and it will depend on the particular needs of the moment in the area concerned whether or not American corn, Ontario corn, or western feed grains are taken. The Wheat Board will be offering, but whether anything is taken or not will be a matter for bargaining.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: I have a final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The minister said that the Wheat Board will be offering. What will happen if the Wheat Board chooses not to offer?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, they have indicated that they will choose to offer. They have so indicated in order to give an assurance to those who might otherwise be concerned about supply. In fact this really only confirms something that has been a policy of long standing, namely, that the Canadian Wheat Board will always protect domestic supply in the sense of not exporting if they leave themselves short. I am surprised that the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) suggested that any other policy was the case. The Wheat Board has always protected Canadian supply and it has no authority to make any change in that policy.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some of my colleagues from the province of Quebec may be wondering whether their region will be affected. As far as I am concerned, I am sure of it because western Quebec is mentioned in the press release and I am very surprised that the government has 
not waited for another review of its freight rates policy. Both ministers have announced they have informed the Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia representatives of this policy, and for the next five years the amounts saved will be spent on livestock and feeds in those areas which will be affected by the removal of transportation subsidies. Mr. Speaker, has the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) a specific program, or is it a study and the program would soon be brought forward, I would be very interested to know whether there is at present a program to assist those regions that will no longer benefit from subsidies to transportation?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a program will be announced I think before August 1. We have done a lot of work on it and have discussed this kind of program with the provinces. The areas that are basically affected are these: the $6 comes off Quebec City at Montreal; Rimouski has a slight reduction to avoid backhaul; there is no reduction in the Gaspe or the Maritimes, and there is no reduction in the Lac-Saint-Jean area of Quebec. We will be publishing a complete detailed form of this within the next couple of days showing exactly how it affects the areas of Quebec that we call western Quebec.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, recently the Canadian Livestock Feed Board suggested that it be given the power to buy and sell so it could establish a price in eastern Canada which the farmer has to pay for the grain. I should like to ask the minister whether he contemplates a seat on the grain exchange for the Canadian Livestock Feed Board in order that it can purchase directly from the market?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in my statement I said if there is evidence of bad pricing or bad supply practices in the market place the Canadian Livestock Feed Board will be permitted to intervene directly in the market, if required, to eliminate such practices.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: One of the reasons why this problem has developed has not been the shortage of supply but the inability of the board to get into a large enough position to supply the market because brokers would not buy early enough to put the grain into the elevators in eastern Canada. What has been done to ensure the farmer that even if we do have additional storage inland in eastern Canada the supplies will be put into position in the elevators by the brokers?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think we recognize that problem in the very fact that we say the grain will be supplied and priced at the competitive Chicago price. We say also that if supplies are not available import permits will be issued for grain if they can find these supplies someplace else. I repeat what I just said, that if there is bad pricing we will allow the Canadian Livestock Feed Board to operate in the market.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister indicated there are to be additional facilities provided under the present system. Mainly we use national harbours, but some other
May 31, 1976

government agencies have elevator space in eastern Canada. Is it the intention to have the new elevator space in eastern Canada under the Canadian Livestock Feed Board, built by them, licensed by them, and operated by them, or how is it anticipated that this storage space will be put into effect? The government is really not going to make any savings if we do not bring grain into eastern Canada by boat, but somebody has to have control and I am wondering if it is to be the feed grain agency.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, feed reserves come under a joint committee made up of various representatives of government agencies, under the chairmanship of the Canadian Livestock Feed Board, and that committee will make recommendations to us in respect of the allocation of stock. A certain small part of the stock is now lying in Halifax, but the balance has been at Thunder Bay. The intention would be to place this in whatever elevators seemed more desirable for moving the supply between these two points.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said that in some cases, as regards supply and prices, the Canadian Feed Board would have authority to intervene. In what way, Mr. Speaker, would the Canadian Feed Board have such authority? With additional funds.? And if the board asks for import permits from the Canadian Wheat Board and the latter say no, which board will take the decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think part of that was just answered in that the Canadian Livestock Feed Board will be involved. If they cannot find ample supplies and there is nothing priced at the proper price the board will be given the authority to enter the market and, if necessary, enter the market outside Canada, which will then require permits to bring the grain back to Canada. Naturally it will be funded by the government in order to be able to do so.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
I have a supplementary.
Mr. Speaker, I asked the following question to the Minister of Agriculture: If the Canadian Feed Board asks for import permits from the Canadian Wheat Board, if the latter rejects its application, will the government intervene either through the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board or through the minister who is responsible for the Canadian Feed Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has the authority under the act. That board operates by order in council, and that is the authority under which it would do
so.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to whichever minister would choose to answer. As I mentioned earlier, the cost of drawing from reserves by eastern feeders was prohibitive. As a result they were transferring grain within regions rather than drawing from reserves supposedly in place. Will that prohibitive cost of drawing from reserves be eliminated and, if so, how will it be done?
Feed Grains

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the rules in relation to feed reserves are carefully set out and are available. It is not our intention that reserves should be drawn upon at any particular moment for no particular reason, because that would interfere with the ordinary placing of stocks into place by those who had the foresight and responsibility to do so. It is, therefore, not considered to be a simple draw-upon with regard to transportation costs, but rather taking them into account in emergencies when stock is available with, of course, a proper accounting for the forward cost of freight.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the minister missed the point of my question. When they found themselves in an emergency position, as I stated in earlier remarks, and had to go to that reserve, the expense was very, very high because of the replacement cost imposed upon them by the Wheat Board or any other replacement agency that might be involved.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the hon. member is confusing the ordinary reserves which the Wheat Board had held in position for export, in which case, when it had to replace those reserves, the real cost to them of replacing them had to be taken into account or it would have been a switch completely at the expense of western grain producers. We are now meeting that problem by establishing a reserve which would be available for the domestic market at domestic prices. That problem in respect of previous switching before we had the reserve arose because the price of that grain was really to be applied at the export price and not at the lower domestic price. At this point in time a switch available at the domestic price will be possible with this reserve in place, as it has been for the past year and a half at Thunder Bay.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of Agriculture. Would the hon. gentleman be able to inform the House of the rate of subsidies for the Rimouski area?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it would take quite a lengthy time to explain what I meant by "backhaul", but it covers the cost of feed at Rimouski because of a backhaul. It will not be the full $6 reduction. This will be outlined in the paper in the next day or two.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the generosity of our two ministers who have maintained part of the subsidies for Gaspesia as it is one area in Quebec which does not produce fodder or livestock.
In view of the fact that starting in August, the subsidies will be discontinued, which will result in an increase of some $6 a ton for feed grains which means $2 more for pork and almost 75 for each chicken, I would like to ask the minister if he is considering setting up a specific program to assist the Ontario and western Quebec cattle raisers?

May 31, 1976
Feed Grains

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the price of grains stayed at the same price as the Chicago corn price there would be a saving to the Gaspe producer who uses western grain of approximately $14 a ton and maybe more, so the $6 would be insignificant. The dairy producer producing dairy products and the poultry producer producing poultry under the present prices would find that the grain they buy would be one of the main input costs they would have to contend with in producing those products, and this would be to their advantage.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have just heard that freight rate assistance on feed grains will be reduced or eliminated and we will have a corn-competitive price. No one said anything about the delivered price. We all know that-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: The hon. member is giving a good imitation of someone making a response on behalf of his party. He is supposed to ask a question. Could he do so now?

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The freight in U.S. haulers is cheaper than in Canada. I put this question to the Minister of Transport. Will this be the delivered price or is the difference in the freight rate of U.S. corn producers to be absorbed by the producers of grain in western Canada, in British Columbia, in Montreal, or especially in the Atlantic provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: When the Wheat Board is selling corn at the competitive price in Montreal the price is then quoted in terms of Thunder Bay, which of course will be the Montreal competitive price less freight. This really means that with feed freight assistance gone in Montreal, the price at Thunder Bay for those who want to feed animals west of there will indeed be $6 a ton lower by the equivalent amount. This tends to mean that the same basis will be used in bringing that grain into grain deficient areas in British Columbia where the lower base price will be the price used by the Canadian Wheat Board in pricing the grain in. In fact that price had been artificially high before because of the effect of feed grain assistance upon the price at Thunder Bay.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Order, please. subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport and it is with regard to what he stated, if I understand him, namely, that the grain position for the export market can be used or tapped in terms of reserve. Given the announced loss of the so-called add a lease rate with respect to grain for export, is there any implication with respect to this on the ultimate price of grain that may have to be taken out of

that stock pile for the local market? In general, what are the implications of the loss of the add a lease rate fairly shortly with respect to feed grains for Nova Scotia or Atlantic region users?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: There is no implication at all because the add a lease rates apply only to the export movement of grain. The fact is that with the retention of feed freight assistance in the Atlantic region at present levels and with the effect upon the price of feed freight being off and therefore off at Thunder Bay, there will be an economic tendency for feed grain to be available at a slightly lower price than would otherwise be the case. I have to stress that in a moving market that would have been the case in the Atlantic region. The feed reserves we have been talking about will be available to be drawn upon and those would ordinarily be priced at their destination plus freight from Thunder Bay. Very often that would be the most economical rate for grain moving there.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: This gives rise to some concern. May I ask the minister whether I can infer from his comments that there will be no overtaxing of storage? I admit the usefulness of it to our own people who might want now, in a stable situation, to use the storage and to buy ahead. Will this overtax our storage capacity for export grains?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, there is really fairly adequate storage. There are some places where additional storage is needed and there are of course DREE efforts to correct the situation directly. There will be further programs in time to improve storage in storage deficient areas in the country.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Agriculture. He is quoted as saying in the press release that the reduction in feed freight assistance should not increase feed grain prices in eastern Canada. Having regard to the fact that feed freight assistance rates will be reduced by $6 a ton, are we to assume that this differential will have to be made up by the producers of grain in western Canada? Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, they are going to meet corn-competitive U.S. prices. That is all we are asking and that is all they have agreed to do.

subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: That is being done now. I am simply asking the minister to confirm or deny the conclusion I have reached. Is it not true that if in fact reduction in feed freight assistance will increase feed grain prices, that the western grain producer will have to make up the differential in order to be competitive, yes or no?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: They asked me a question, Mr. Speaker, and then they tell me how to answer it. I think that is going a little far. The price of feed grain will be the same for the western producer exactly as it will be for the eastern producer. The hon. member was talking about British Columbia. This year they brought in ten times more American corn to British Columbia than they did the year before. The producers of livestock and grain will be on a more equitable basis.

Mr. Speaker, I was not jumping up and down earlier because there were so many others and I have had one kick at the cat, but I would like to ask two questions in one, in order to take account of your kind indulgence.
First, since the Minister of Agriculture did not quite answer the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski) I will ask a question of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. In relation to U.S. corn prices now the statement says "Because western grains are going to be available at corn-competitive prices, I do not expect the reduction in feed freight assistance to increase feed grain prices in eastern Canada or British Columbia."
In relation to U.S. corn prices now, can the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board tell us what effect that will have on barley, oats or feed wheat in relation to Canadian Wheat Board prices? Will it not mean a reduction in the price to western Canadian grain producers?
Second, would the minister now tell us what he is thinking about in terms of a plebiscite, which has been asked for, regarding feed grains in the open market? Is he now prepared to call one?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS ON FEED GRAIN POLICY BY MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND BY MINISTER OF TRANSPORT
speechtext:
While we are clearly getting closer to that point there remain one or two items under the feed grain policy which still have to be put into effect before it is fully there, but I think it is becoming better understood and operating more fully now. When the sale of grain in question is Wheat Board grain at corn-competitive prices rather than grain farmer to farmer or region to region on a direct basis, which is still possible and raises different issues, then the effect of not having the artificial feed freight assistance to the Montreal and Ontario regions is to lower the price at Thunder Bay by that amount, and therefore also to lower the price of feed grains in the elevators to the buyer of those feed grains who raise animals in western Canada. It is exactly that.
It is the removal of an artificial factor which had been distorting natural advantage, and I was always pleased to note that the western organizations discussing this subject did not divide on product lines, but the grain farmer and the meat farmer joined together in wanting this artificial factor removed.
