speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the five o'clock adjournment I was beginning a quotation from the second reading debate in 1961 of the remarks of the then minister of justice, as follows:
Society's concern for its basic rules is expressed in its commands and corresponding sanctions that together constitute our criminal law. The degree of society's concern with respect to individual rules is reflected in the method of expression adopted. In this sense, therefore, the sanction for the law against murder may properly reflect the importance which society attaches to the maintenance of that law. In our view, Canadians properly attach so high a value to the sanctity of human life that the law which translates this feeling into effective form should provide the maximum sanction for its deliberate breach, and no other penalty would be considered adequate.
In my view those remarks of the Hon. David Fulton in 1961 have as clear an application today as they did then. In fact the Canadian people reflect an even higher concern, and it is for that reason that we see from one end of the country to the other this expression of public opinion-not just by a minor margin, not by 10 per cent, not by 20 per cent-in proportions of 80 per cent of 90 per cent for the retention of capital punishment and the carrying out of the law.
What does Bill C-84 do? For one thing, of course, it abolishes the word "capital." It abolishes capital murder and non capital murder because it wants to get away from that. So we are going to get Hawaii Five-O's and all the multitude of American police television programs' versions of murder one and murder two. It will be great to hear them calling out, "Book him on murder one", in the most dramatic voice!
But what is being substituted for the equivalent of capital murder is a sentence of 25 years and the possibility, under certain circumstances, of an individual applying for parole after somewhere between 15 and 18 years. In other words, these people are to be put into a jail and the key effectively thrown away.
Much is said about rehabilitation. There is not one person, here in this Chamber or outside, who can say that a

man having served 15 or 18 years is rehabilitated. He has become so institutionalized and so bereft of the practice of living in ordinary society that he cannot be rehabilitated.
Man is strange; but perhaps I am a little subjective with regard to being incarcerated. I have not done time in any prison, but I was a prisoner of war for nearly three years. Even during that time some individuals acted with great desperation and tried to break out. They were reckless about their safety and one or two that I know unfortunately never made it back, not even in a "klim tin" because they were liquidated. On the other hand, I know that if any of us in the camp that I was in, or those in scores of other camps in Germany, or those in the hands of the Japanese, had been told that we were to be there for life, there were three options for a great number of people. They could hang themselves or do away with themselves in a sheer blue funk. I have seen this happen to men who could not stand the pressure. Another option was to take the life of a guard, in desperation. What could a man lose under those circumstances?
How can one pile 25 years on top of 25 years and make it meaningful? This is the attitude of the wolves in prison- what do they have to lose if all they are going to get is a further life sentence? Is it going to be incarceration in solitary, in segregated custody? Now the do-gooders and the bleeding hearts and the nice Nellies complain about isolation in the newspapers, on television, everywhere. They say solitary confinement is inhumane, but in many cases protective custody will be the only answer. What about Williams and the chap in Saskatoon? What about many other cases where we know there has been a dastardly crime, particularly when it involves children? Those people have to be put in isolation if they are to live, but on the whole society says we are not going to kill them-we will eliminate capital punishment, we will just turn them over to the wolves in prisons and they can do a job of capital punishment.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: What about-

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Just listen.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has the floor.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote against this bill because I support capital punishment. Those who insist on the right to life and say that the state has no right to take a life should consider the victims. Did they not have a right to life? Surely the person who has wrongfully taken the life or lives of others has forfeited his absolute right. To me, Mr. Speaker, the substitution of life imprisonment is even worse. It is coldly sadistic in so many instances.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Is it agreed?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Agreed.
May 31, 1976

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: I shall finish in a moment, Mr. Speaker. I respect the right of others to hold a contrary opinion, and many do; however, I resent the high moral tone of so many so-called abolitionists who somehow or other feel they have been called upon to wrap around themselves a self-fashioned cloak of some alleged higher morality, whether Christian or otherwise. Who says theirs is a higher morality? Then there are those who allege that the abolition of capital punishment is the characteristic of a civilized society. Who says so? Only an abolitionist. Is a retentionist, to use the simplistic term, any less civilized? The burden of proof in any argument in favour of the abolition of capital punishment rests on those who wish to make the change. Mr. Speaker, in my opinion they have failed to discharge the burden of proof imposed upon them.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was curious about the last few remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) in view of the lecture he gave us this afternoon because I imagine he was quoting something.
I participate in this debate because I should like to propose a number of solutions that I do not think have been discussed. Members who have spoken on both sides of the debate have been sincere, have reasoned and wrestled over a period of time with their consciences. They have considered the information supplied by their constituents and to a large extent the testimony of those who appeared before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs on at least four occasions in the last eight or ten years. They have taken a position honestly, in my opinion.
Many members do not believe in the idea of consensus. Few have suggested, with any degree of honesty, a desire to have a plebiscite on this issue. If they really believed that, then they would have a plebiscite on everything. As all members know, circumstances change, situations change, many arguments are based upon personal experience, and happily those arguments change many times too.
I can remember a few debates where a definite opinion was taken by all members of the House. On the War Measures Act a few were on one side, the majority on the other. I can honestly say with hindsight that maybe the majority was wrong and the very small minority was right.
The flag debate was another of those emotional subjects on which one forms an opinion based on background. Now we have a flag and it is fairly well accepted by most of the country. I was rather surprised a couple of weeks ago when driving on the road to my home to see a Union Jack on a flagpole. I wondered why he was not flying the Ontario flag, until my wife reminded me it was the Queen's birthday. Probably that was why he was flying the Union Jack. We debated the issue of the Canadian flag. Certainly the country does not begrudge our discussing those issues, and does not begrudge exchanges which take place in the heat of debate. But once we decide, the country accepts our decision, knowing very well that we may modify our decision from time to time.
I have always been of the opinion that we should not hang people. I have heard members suggest that we should use the guillotine instead of a rope. Well, I oppose the use
Capital Punishment
of the guillotine, the use of the electric chair, the use of the firing squad, etc. Rightly or wrongly I think society has less right to take a life than an individual has, if an individual has such right. When a man kills another, he probably does it for some reason. But society executes on the excuse that it protects. I have heard it suggested that society executes out of revenge. Be that as it may, I say that any society which executes is none too civilized.
This afternoon the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) used the example of a man who raped, then murdered a couple of young children. Surely a layman could only conclude that the man was not in his right mind. Sane people do not do that; therefore hanging them or putting them in jail for life is not the civilized way of curing the problem. People like that probably need medical attention. They should be confined in an institution for the insane, not imprisoned in a penitentiary for life.
I agree with what has been said about the cabinet's commuting death sentences. I agree that since we retained the death penalty for the murders of prison guards and policemen those convicted of such crimes should have been executed-save and except in cases when the cabinet's prerogative of mercy could be properly exercised. The cabinet did not choose to allow any murderers to be executed, which I think was wrong.
I am concerned about how the different categories of murderers are to be treated. In my opinion the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has brought in few, if any, reforms. He has done little in the field of penal reform, or in any other field for that matter. Why Mr. Speaker? The government is backward, cautious, and totally incompetent in this regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Surely the hon. member does not mean that.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Yes I do. It is totally incompetent. Actually it is going backwards, like a kid trying to pedal a bicycle when the chain has fallen off.
The previous hon. member who spoke said that he thought a 25-year sentence of imprisonment for murder is more barbaric than hanging. I agree.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: It is 15 years.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: With respect, it is 25.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Look at the bill again.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
How can we expect judges to render impartial decisions when we clamour for 25-year sentences? Only on the most rare occasion will a judge impose a sentence of less than 25 years. It seems to me that the 25-year sentence is probably the most barbaric penalty our system can meet out. Consider the feelings of a person of, say, 40 years who faces a 25-year prison term. He knows he is without hope of release and will make no contribution at all to society. I am prepared to support the idea that a man should be sent to jail for 25 years, on this condition-that he be provided with a potassium cyanide capsule so that if he feels his punishment is intolerable he can take his own life. There must be safeguards, of course, to make sure that the capsule does not end up in the warden's soup. Prisoners have been known not to like wardens.

May 31, 1976
Capital Punishment
I suggest that if the prisoner feels he cannot face a jail term of 25 years he should have the right to take his own life. Society should not make that decision for him. Actually secret service agents now are provided with potassium cyanide capsules. After a United States spy plane was shot down by the Russians, a United States committee which investigated the case suggested that if Gary Powers had swallowed a lethal pill he would have avoided all the fuss and embarrassment which followed his capture. If hon. members were to propose the retention of the death penalty in the form I propose, I might support such a bill. But I cannot support the idea of imprisoning a man for 25 years, without any hope of release.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: It's 15 years.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) insists it is 15 years. I suggest that he is not aware of the changes taking place in present day society.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: The hon. member is not aware of the provisions of the bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: It is interesting to note that when skirts get longer, society feels insecure. At present our citizens are concerned about personal security and loss of income. We have not seen such fear for some time. Normally hemlines come down either before or during a war or just before a serious recession. Most of the 700,000-odd unemployed think the recession is here, now. People want collective security. As I said, when recession is upon us, hemlines drop. When hemlines go up, it means things are free and easy.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
But when they start coming down, watch out. They are a pretty good economic indicator. I suggest to the hon. member for New Westminster that as time passes, our judges will become more and more conservative and react more to the general tone of society as society becomes less progressive and people draw together for collective security. They will be more like the Ku Klux Klan five years from now than the progressive judges of five or ten years ago. They react to the society they are in, the same as members of parliament.
We have paid no attention to the protection of society. We spend a lot of money to keep people in jail. Every once in a while the Solicitor General announces that a new penitentiary will be built. Statistics indicate that there are more people in jail in Canada than in any other civilized country. That is no honour.
I have visited some of our penitentiaries on numerous occasions. I met many of the prisoners, guards, and officials. I was pleased with the changes that were being made in the penitentiary system a few years ago, but since that time very little has been done. As a matter of fact since Commissioner McLeod left the penitentiary service there has been very little progressive thought in the whole service. He had faults, there is no question about that. However, he had an excellent mind and knew more about criminology than most people. His dream was that by the

time he left the penitentiary service more people would be rehabilitated than when he took over.
There has been very little progress with regard to rehabilitation. Society is scared. Any time someone does not return after being granted a leave, the Solicitor General is jumped on. When he tries to explain, he puts his foot in his mouth and the problem sounds worse than it did originally.
When there was a problem at Millhaven two members of parliament visited there. I was one of them. That section of the act that permitted members of parliament to visit a penitentiary at reasonable times was removed by a former Solicitor General. That had been a British tradition, but we had a non-British Solicitor General. He felt that the visits caused problems, and therefore members could no longer visit a penitentiary without his permission.
Since that time I have not visited a penitentiary. If I cannot go there on my own to talk to those people and intervene if necessary, I am not going to go. I suggest there are many members who have never visited a penitentiary. They should do so.
It cost $20,000 a year to keep a person in jail. The government is now talking about keeping murderers in jail for 25 years. At $20,000 a year that is a fairly expensive proposition.
In my limited experience I have found that it is often easier to rehabilitate a murderer than any other type of prisoner. It is very difficult to rehabilitate a dope addict, forger of con artist. It is almost impossible to rehabilitate a bank robber. In many cases a murderer could be set free the day after his trial. There are lawyers here who know that. Even though the murder may have been premeditated, it was carried out under extreme provocation. That provocation likely would not occur again during that person's lifetime.
One day you have a good citizen with no criminal intent and no criminal record. He commits a murder. He is either sentenced to jail for life or executed. In my experience it would be easy to rehabilitate that person.
I think I have told the story before of intervening on behalf of a young man who committed an atrocious murder. He was released. After five years he completed his course at Queen's University. That man is now married and has a number of children. I am sure he will never again be in trouble. I believe that story could be repeated by lawyers hundreds of times.
A law abiding citizen may commit a murder. However, the chances of that happening are very small. The chance of him committing a second murder is almost nil. His neighbour is more likely to commit murder than he is likely to murder a second time.
This must be explained to society. The little old lady walking through the park believes that if we execute the murderer, she will not have her purse snatched. I fail to see the relationship, but she understands it. She believes there is a total breakdown in society. This fits in with the change that I see in society.
A few years ago we changed the homosexual laws, abortion laws, and divorce laws. A number of changes were made in the social field. I respectfully suggest those
May 31, 1976

changes could not be made today because society would not allow it. Society is moving very far to the right. If members of parliament are going to be limited in that way with regard to changes in society, all we really need is a machine and we can let the public vote. Everyone could vote on every subject. There could be vigilante committees established all over the place, such as there are in some countries. The strong will be right and the weak will be eliminated. Surely that is not civilized society.
We must not only look at what we are doing with regard to capital punishment but with regard to the rehabilitation of prisoners. Many of these prisoners could be sent to our "Siberia". We need a highway to the Arctic, as well as a pipeline down the west shore of Hudson's Bay. This involves a great deal of work. Why not have the prisoners do it? We hear about Christian principles. One Calvinistic principle that is very strong in Canadian society is that work is good and to work makes you good. If that has any merit it would work well with some of our prisoners.
Our prisoners are only given very menial tasks, if any. Time weighs heavily in their hands. They scheme, plan, and do all sorts of things. However, they are not being rehabilitated. There are many jobs in the Arctic that could be done by machine, but there is still a great deal of manual labour required. If we are going to have sovereignty in the Arctic, we need to build airports. We would not need guards for these prisoners, only foremen. The prisoners would be paid for their work. In addition, they would develop a trade that could be marketed when they return to society. If they were willing to accept the discipline necessary in that environment, they could be rehabilitated. If not, they would again be sent there.
Surely it would be possible to develop a work program which would lead to the rehabilitation of a great many prisoners, allowing them to return to society making use of the trades they have been taught while in prison. You do not have to go much further than my new riding, Mr. Speaker. You would not need any guards there. If you were to leave the area you would be eaten alive by mosquitoes or drown in the muskeg. For nine months of the year you would be frozen to death.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: What riding are you speaking of?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: I am speaking of the area north of Moosonee. I question the minister's attitude. He seems to take great pride in building a new penitentiary every few months.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: He announces one.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Well, he announces it and keeps moving it around from one riding to another. I have known him for some time. He is a very honest person and a very dedicated person. I am sure that many of the goals he has in mind could be achieved. But what we have to find is some way of reducing our prison population. The reason they are in penitentiaries is because they cannot adjust to the demands of society. Surely it is necessary to train them in such a way as to make them fit for release into society. This change in approach must be made known in such a way as to make everyone in the country familiar with it. If this is done sympathy will be developed and the public
Capital Punishment
generally will be in a better position to understand the achievements and problems of a penal reform system.
It is not good enough merely to read from time to time a newspaper headline announcing that a prisoner has escaped while on leave to attend his mother's funeral. The department must be prepared to state plainly that last year thousands of people were allowed out of prison on a weekly basis to rejoin their families with the result that, when the time for their release came, they were much better prepared to return to their communities in a different frame of mind. Obviously this is easier for them if they are familiar with the life of the community as it is today rather than it was five or six years ago, before they went to jail, or else they would return to it as if it were a foreign environment.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: What do you mean by "foreign environment"?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
I did not hear that interruption but it was probably made by someone who had looked at all the difficulties and had never considered any of the advantages.
When Commissioner MacLeod was in charge the character of many of our penal institutions was changed. From being merely jails with security guards they became institutions where prisoners were given advice and helped in every way possible to develop a sense of responsibility to the community.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: I paid particular attention to the hon. member's comment concerning the day parole system-he spoke of its success and the need to develop it further. In the light of his evident approval of that program as carried out by the Department of the Solicitor General I was wondering how he could justify his earlier statement that the policies of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) had been a total failure.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Shame. You have given him another hour!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Perhaps I should not have said they were a total failure. The day parole system has been in effect for some time. It has been expanded so as to allow people out of prison to attend educational institutions. What I am saying is that the minister has not developed any system which was not already in effect. I am suggesting, too, that he has done very little to explain some of his problems. I have in mind an occasion when one particular incident was disclosed, and the minister threw in two or three more that nobody knew about, and then the fat was in the fire. He has done that on a number of occasions.
If the Solicitor General does have any new proposals he certainly has not told people about them. All I ever read in the papers is his intention to build a new jail somewhere. If any evidence of his own attitude to some of these situations were needed one need look no further than the subject of the present debate. Murderers are not to be hanged but they are to be put in jail for 25 years. Under the

May 31, 1976
Capital Punishment
old system, Mr. Speaker, some of them got out after five years and, in my opinion, they were totally rehabilitated. In my view, that is possible. Mr. Speaker, if there were anything which might make me consider voting for hanging it would be the length of the sentence the minister is proposing.
If the hon. gentleman really wants to get this debate over, one way would be to arrange for eight or ten hangings on July 1 on the front lawn of the Parliament Buildings with coverage in colour television. I am sure he would then have no problem.
I am sure that if you asked most people who are in favour of hanging whether they would be prepared, as a member of a jury, where each vote counts, to bring in a verdict which would ensure such a penalty, they would tell you they wanted no part of such a decision. Nevertheless they are willing to allow society to make such a decision for them, and they do so because they fear hard times are coming and they are scared; they are willing to accept any measures which it is felt might protect them. Members of parliament, even those who believe there is a certain role for vengeance, a certain role for deterrence can only do that in good conscience, surely, if they are prepared to adopt a totally different way of eliminating the people society wishes to reject.
In my area not long ago a man hung a dog to a clothesline with a piece of wire. He was taken to court and received a two-year sentence for cruelty. I do not think he served any time in jail. It was a suspended sentence. But he got two years for hanging that dog. We are being asked to do that in the name of society. On occasion a man hangs from the gallows and suffocates for up to eight or 10 minutes before he dies. And we call ourselves a civilized society! I would question that, and so would anyone who witnesses such a barbaric way of disposing of people.
I would sacrifice the six or eight people who are now on death row awaiting passage of this legislation by hanging them in front of the Parliament Buildings on July 1 to celebrate our development as a "civilized society" because, Mr. Speaker, there would be such revulsion against that act that there is no question that the Canadian public would support the abolition of the death penalty, and of that method in particular, forever.
If we are to keep people in jail for 25 years, which is the period the minister has had to settle for, we should also provide them with the means of leaving this world. To me, this is just as barbaric as eliminating them. We should let these people make a choice between the two.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: How about giving them a colour TV?

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
The hon. member says we should give them a colour television set. No doubt some people in that category would appreciate a colour television set. If we are giving them away we should give them to other institutions, not penal institutions. We could put these people to work in the uranium mines at Eldorado or wherever they may be. Let us pay them a good wage. Certainly this would not cost us as much as keeping them in solitude, without hope, without reform, without fitting them for a return to society. In many instances we make sure that these people will

remain in penal institutions for the rest of their lives; they will continue to return to them because our penal system makes them even less fitted for society outside.
I suggest we give reform serious consideration. The minister should ask members of parliament to pass some progressive legislation in the field of penal reform. Reformation of our prisoners and of those who have offended against society should be made an important part of our legal structure. If it is not, we will continue to have the unenviable record of having the largest number of people in jail per population of any country in the western world.
Despite this retrograde step it seems to me that the minister still has some support in the House for progressive legislation. If that is not the case, if he has frittered it away, then the three or four votes for abolition that I have heard today will go down the drain, just as did the larger number that we had on the last occasion. The amendment that may be moved by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) may in the end have to be the solution if the minister does not give some consideration to putting members of parliament in the picture about what he hopes to do. He should not attempt to satisfy public opinion by passing a stupid piece of legislation. Better that it is not passed than to perpetrate a hoax in the form of these long mandatory sentences, which in many cases will not be served and will certainly not serve society for the next three or four years before the law is once again changed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is slightly more than three years since I last had the opportunity of speaking on this subject.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
I see that my absence has been noted by the other side. As a matter of fact I last spoke on this subject on May 29, 1973. We heard today that about 70 members of this Chamber have participated so far in the debate on Bill C-84, which I guess the government House leader considers to be quite a number. Nevertheless this means that less than one third of the members of the House have so far taken the opportunity of expressing their opinion on a subject of very deep concern to the general public of this country. I hope a way will be found to enable practically all members to have an opportunity of stating their positions on the capital punishment question.
A number of the Canadian people are beginning to wonder about the efficacy of the principle of representative government. Opinion polls-I know the government spends a lot of money on and pays a lot of attention to polls-indicate that Canadians in general want the principle of capital punishment retained as the law of this land. They are very concerned about the recent attitude of the government which ignores with impunity one of the basic laws of the land. Somehow or other the members of this Chamber will have to pay some attention to the question of representing the population of Canada, though I know some of them hate to be reminded that they are representatives.
I see Your Honour is moving in your chair and it is about ten o'clock, so may I call it ten o'clock and continue on Friday?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-LOCKHEED CONTRACT-DEPARTMENT'S KNOWLEDGE OF FINANCING DIFFICULTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the Minister of National Defence's (Mr. Richardson) handling of the LRPA purchase can hardly be termed competent, his colleagues in cabinet have shown no great skill either, except in attempting to put all the blame on the Minister of National Defence's shoulders.
In interviews over the Victoria Day weekend, and again in the House on Tuesday, May 25, and Friday, May 28, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) let it be known that he did not think much of a process whereby multi-million dollar contracts were agreed to on the basis of nothing more than a verbal agreement between two individuals that financing would be available.
At the time the deal collapsed the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) also indicated that the source of the problem was that cabinet had been told Lockheed could provide the money. Each conveniently forgets that not only did the Minister of National Defence believe in the verbal agreement, but the whole cabinet apparently believed in it too.
Adjournment Debate
Not one cabinet minister, least of all the Minister of Supply and Services, has said he looked for a written assurance before Lockheed was authorized on December 2 to start work on the contract.
In addition to all the blame for the verbal agreement being pushed on the Minister of National Defence and "a general" whom one assumes is General Allan, the manager of the LRPA project office, we also have the interesting spectacle of the Minister of Supply and Services saying he did not know the Department of National Defence was short of funds, nor that Lockheed had agreed to provide these funds when he authorized work to begin. I refer to Hansard of March 29 at page 12217. Later he said that officials in his department were not aware of these facts either which, given the relationship of the project office to the Department of Supply and Services, is surely asking too much of our credulity.
The story, as it has emerged so far, is that the project office negotiated a contract for 18 LRPA's. Though the project manager was General Allan from the Department of National Defence, the deputy project manager, with principal responsibility for negotiating the terms of the contract, was L. H. Stopforth, an official from the Department of Supply and Services. As Mr. Crutchlow, the assistant deputy minister of the Department of National Defence explained to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence on March 23, at page 33:30:
-the contract has been negotiated by the contract office. That office, as the minister has said, is led by General Allan as the project manager, but his deputy is a member of the Department of Supply and Services, a senior officer of that department. He is primarily responsible for the actual composition of the contract, along with his line branches that work in the DSS.
The project office negotiated with Lockheed a contract based on Lockheed's most cost-effective schedule and based also on the premise that there would be more money available in the defence budget. As it turned out this was a mistaken premise, for it was only in November that cabinet gave consideration to the long term budget, and it was only at that time it became apparent there would be shortfalls in 1976-77 and in the two subsequent years. I refer to General Allan's evidence to the standing committee on April 13, 1976, at page 35:9.
General Allan said that when it was realized there would be a shortfall "we" contacted both suppliers, Boeing and Lockheed, and asked whether they could finance the shortfall, and both replied in the affirmative. It was on this basis that cabinet documentation was prepared. I refer to General Allan's evidence to the standing committee on April 13, 1976, at page 35:7. When asked about this on Thursday, May 27, General Allan told the standing committee that he personally made the phone calls to Boeing and Lockheed, and the results of these conversations were reported to his deputy, Mr. Stopforth.
The whole organization of the project office makes it appear very unlikely that the Minister of Supply and Services did not know of the financial problems of the Department of National Defence. General Allan explained to the standing committee on May 13, as reported at page 39:6, that he was responsible to the deputy ministers of four departments; Defence, Supply and Services, Industry, Trade and Commerce, and DREE. He reported to the deputy ministers through a senior management board,

May 31, 1976
Adjournment Debate
which had representation at the assistant deputy minister level from the four departments concerned. This senior management board was chaired by Mr. Crutchlow, assistant deputy minister of the Department of National Defence.
When asked whether the Department of National Defence's lack of money and Lockheed's verbal commitment to provide financing were communicated to this management board, General Allan said:
Yes, the senior management board was aware of that, as were the cabinet and the Treasury Board, that we had a shortfall between the funds that were available to the Department of National Defence and the cash flow that was required in the contract which had been negotiated in this case with Lockheed, in our judgment.
When asked whether cabinet also was aware of Lockheed's verbal commitment, General Allan said:
Yes, our judgment in the recommendations we made up the line was that this we could negotiate with Lockheed to solve this shortfall in the cash between what was available and what was required in the contract.
On Thursday, May 27, General Allan was even more specific about who knew about the shortfall and the verbal promise that financing would be available. He said:
The phone calls to both Boeing and Lockheed were made by myself. The results of those conversations were reported back into the project office to my deputy. The gist of the conversations were put in the submission to cabinet; they were put in a submission to Treasury Board; the cabinet submission was dated November 14 and was considered by cabinet on November 27; the Treasury Board submission was briefed on the basis of a draft document on November 27; the formal Treasury Board submission for the program was on December 1. The shortfall was pointed out in all these documents. There was a briefing prepared for the Department of Supply and Services on November 30 to ... my understanding was that the Deputy Minister of Supply and Services briefed the Minister on December 1.

subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-LOCKHEED CONTRACT-DEPARTMENT'S KNOWLEDGE OF FINANCING DIFFICULTIES
speechtext:
Including the shortfall.
Gen. Allan: Including the shortfall.
The Minister of National Defence intervened here to support General Allan. He said:
To confirm what Brigadier General Allan has said the fact that cabinet approved interest payments and which as I said are in the blue book, indicates that cabinet knew there was a shortfall. If they were not going to finance anything then they would not need interest payments. So, I am just confirming what General Allan has said. This was known to the cabinet and certainly known to any minister who was at cabinet.
This comment is interesting in view of the Minister of Supply and Services' repeated statements that he negotiated on the assumption that since DND placed the order it had the money available. Though one does not know whether the Minister of Supply and Services was actually at the cabinet meeting on November 27, is it not very unusual that he was not informed of the results of that meeting, either by a colleague, or through circulation of the minutes? In other words, even if one ignores General Allan's testimony that officials from DSS, including Mr. Stopforth and the Deputy minister, knew these facts, how was it possible for the Minister of Supply and Services not to know that DND was short of funds?
General Allan's comments bring into sharper focus the contrast between what DND says, and what DSS says. Given the organization of the project office, one would assume that the whole project team, not just those members from DND, knew about the shortage of funds, and General Allan has indicated he did tell Mr. Stopforth.

Certainly Mr. Stopforth knew about DND's shortfall in the previous year since he wrote the letters to Mr. Heppe of Lockheed inquiring about alternatives, and there appears to be no reason why he would not have been told about the 1976-77 shortfall and the attempts to overcome it.
However, the Minister of Supply and Services claims that Mr. Stopforth did not know about the shortage of funds for 1976-77 and Lockheed's verbal assurance that it could provide financing; he told the House on Tuesday, May 25, in answer to my question, that he did not know whether the information had been deliberately kept from Mr. Stopforth but,
... be that as it may, the representative of my department on the management committee of that project was not advised of the possibility of that financial arrangement.
The Minister of Supply and Services did not answer the second part of my question, which is whether his deputy minister knew of the shortfall problem. Again because of the structure of the project office, and General Allan's testimony, it seems to me that the deputy minister of Supply and Services must have known.
The misunderstanding with Lockheed, as the Minister of National Defence likes to call it, arose in the period from December 2 to December 22, when Lockheed told General Allan that it could not provide the financing after all.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-LOCKHEED CONTRACT-DEPARTMENT'S KNOWLEDGE OF FINANCING DIFFICULTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the LRPA project has a significant involvement for four departments: DND which as the user of the defence supplies is responsible for funding the requirement and defining the specification, DSS which as the procurement authority in the government negotiates and administers the contract, ITC which determines and evaluates Canadian industrial benefits, and DREE which applies its concern to realize opportunities for regional economic development that might flow from a major procurement such as the LRPA. Accordingly, because of the multi-departmental interests a project office was established to ensure good management among the four departments directly involved. Staff from the concerned departments were co-located in one office to do the job in a unified and effective manner, taking into account the responsibilities of their respective department. Because DND has the main involvement and interest, the project leader was selected from that department.
The organization of the project office reflected the functional interests of the four departments and contained the following elements: operational; technical; logistical; contractual; industrial development; regional economic development. These six elements worked together in the one office to administer the project.
The LRPA project had three phases to it. In Phase I starting November 1, 1972, five contractors submitted proposals for an Argus replacement. This phase was unfunded. Phase II commenced on May 6, 1974, but only included two, not five, contractors. During this phase Boeing and Lockheed were funded in the amounts of $5.5 million and $5.7
May 31, 1976

million respectively to define the LRPA requirements. This phase was completed in November, 1975. Phase III covering the design, development, production, test and delivery by the successful bidder was to commence when a definitive contract was placed.
DND has always been responsible for funding all contract demands or requisitions sent to DSS or its predecessors for procurement of defence goods and services. This responsibility lies within their internal delegation of authority for program funding. It is not or never has been a DSS responsibility.
The LRPA project was duly approved by Treasury Board and cabinet and was ready to proceed to the contract stage. The Department of National Defence was responsible for providing the necessary funds out of their capital budget. Because of a non-recorded conversation which the project manager had with an official of Lockheed, it was assumed that DND funding would be supplemented by some financing from Lockheed.
As things developed, this possibility did not materialize, and this is why Lockheed proceeded to attempt to interest a Canadian bank consortium to make the funds available through the assignment of the contract.
Officials of DND are responsible for managing their capital budget and this was entirely their responsibility. The question of a shortfall of cash to be financed by Lockheed did not become known to the minister and to the senior management of DSS until January.
The reason for issuing a telex on December 2 was to preserve the price, deliveries, and industrial off-set benefits contained in the Lockheed offer before the offer expired on December 2, 1975. This is normal procedure until all the clauses of the contract have been finally developed in legal terms and are agreed fully in detail by both parties. Up to the time the financing problem arose there was reasonable assumption that the contract could be signed in the middle of January.
As it turned out, considerable delay was involved in the negotiations between Lockheed and the Canadian banks as to the possibility of financing and, while these negotiations were going on, it was essential to protect the price, deliveries and off-set conditions on a week to week basis.
Eventually, an option agreement was signed with Lockheed when the possibility of Canadian bank financing appeared reasonably certain.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: TRANSPORT-INCREASE IN CONTAINER FREIGHT RATES- REQUEST FOR REVIEW BY TRANSPORT COMMISSION OR GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION
TRANSPORT-INCREASE IN CONTAINER FREIGHT RATES- REQUEST FOR REVIEW BY TRANSPORT COMMISSION OR GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that was an awful lot of balderdash we just listened to, but my concern is the movement of container traffic out of the port of Halifax and Saint John into central Canada, and specifically the proposed freight rate increases on containers to be effective on July 1.
Within the United Kingdom and the continental area of northern Europe there is a freight conference of lines serving the east coast Canadian ports which permits shippers to charge the same ocean freight rates as those serving the ports of Montreal and Toronto directly. In other words, it does not cost any more to ship by way of Halifax than it does by way of Montreal or Toronto into those particular destinations.
This saving has been dependent upon the cost charged to the carriers by the CN system, which in fact is the captive shipper. Without getting into the difficulties which lay behind the questions we asked-the disastrous rate wars in the North Atlantic in 1972 and 1973, the resolution of these problems in 1974 by the introduction of agreements between the Canadian and American lines which permitted cargo to move freely to and from Canada by way of U.S. ports provided Canadian rates were charged, and again with respect to American lines which were permitted to absorb the inland trucking costs from Montreal and Toronto and their base ports in the United States-in spite of this the cargoes continued to flow by way of the United States for a substantial period of time. Indeed we are now looking at some 60,000 tons of cargo going by way of U.S. ports, and in a down period in the movement of containers in the North Atlantic conference we notice that while Canada's total number-and we will use the units, the 20, 35 and 40 foot units-has been down in the period of the last couple of years, probably reflecting trends in world trade, we notice that movement through U.S. ports has not been down.
There is a reason for this, and the reason, of course, lies in the fears that we on the east coast have with respect to the increase in the cost of moving containers, an increase of 7 per cent in the cost of moving containers from Halifax and Saint John into Montreal and Toronto. This increase has been imposed at a point in time when no similar increase is being imposed upon other movers.
Of course any mover of freight has to absorb the total cost of the particular piece of freight permitted under the rules of the North Atlantic Conference with no opportunity for movers on the east coast, for example, to absorb the 7 per cent increase in cost which must perforce come out of their ability to earn dollars. All the 7 per cent increase will do, particularly with respect to the 40 foot containers moving from Saint John and Halifax, is place

May 31, 1976
Adjournment Debate
them in a competitive position with the ports of Montreal and Toronto through the Port of New York which can in turn offer about a 1'A or 3 VS day advantage in time over the Port of Halifax. Time being dollars with respect to the movement of cargo, it will not go any other route than through the Port of New York. This is what we are afraid of if the government permits Canadian National to impose the additional 7 per cent.
The problem is compounded by the fact that it is the United States east coast ports that traffic out of Saint John and Halifax will move and not other east Canadian ports. There would be no advantage for large ships that use the ports of Halifax and Saint John to try to get into Montreal or Toronto because they would lose the advantage of the large size containers, which is part of the way that entrepreneurs moving containers in world traffic find the margin for profit.
I should like to see the government review this situation from the point of view of the movement of these containers through Canadian ports. For example, Dart, ACL, Hapag Lloyd or any other line are not in a position to take their customers and get an increase in rates. They cannot do that under the terms of the conference until some time next March or April. It is now the end of May and the increase faces us on July 1. If we are to ask the shippers of 40 foot containers from Halifax to absorb 7 per cent and take into consideration the fact that Dart Lines own about 60 per cent of the port facility at Port Elizabeth in New Jersey, they are not going to move through Halifax. They are going to move their 40 foot containers through their own ports into Montreal and Toronto. They can use the single rate based upon trail of usage.
We would like to get some kind of deferral of any increase until such time as the shipper is in a position to go to his customer and get the appropriate increase to absorb the increase in rail cost. Short of that it would only be fair if the government were to consider an increase in cost to those using the Port of Montreal or the Port of Toronto with respect to the movement of containers and the Con-rail service from New York into either Toronto or Montreal. Essentially those are the two points I wished to make.
It is unfair to the people of Halifax and Saint John to put shippers using the ports in the position in which they must absorb out of their own profits the full 7 per cent when a similar amount is not imposed on those using other ports directly and CN is not imposing such increases on movements from New York to Toronto and Montreal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-INCREASE IN CONTAINER FREIGHT RATES- REQUEST FOR REVIEW BY TRANSPORT COMMISSION OR GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) for the analysis of the freight rate situation which he placed on the record of the House this evening. I assure him that I will make certain that all the factors he brought forward this evening will be brought to the attention of the responsible authorities both within the Department of Transport and outside, and I hope they will conduct a full analysis of the important concerns he raised this evening.
Originally, when my hon. friend addressed his question to me in the minister's absence during the question period,

it had to do with the impact, if any, which the anti-inflation program might have on the specific freight rate increases to which he alluded. Essentially the hon. member asked me at that time whether the government intends to ensure that the Canadian Transport Commission will review the increase in container freight rates out of the ports of Halifax and Saint John into Montreal. The short answer is, yes.
I remind the hon. member that under the anti-inflation legislation the Canadian Transport Commission has responsibility for monitoring increases in freight, passenger, and express rates, and the increases in revenues to be derived therefrom. It is carrying out those duties which, among other things, require it to report to the governor in council where, in the opinion of the Commission, an action on the part of the railways is likely to lead to a breach of the guidelines.
I should like to confirm to my hon. friend that the commission is monitoring the recent increase in the container freight rates from Halifax and Saint John to Montreal and Toronto and has called on the railways to furnish it with all the information it requires in the pursuit of its anti-inflation duties.
As I said earlier, I will ensure that the important considerations my hon. friend described to the House are brought to the attention of responsible officials in order that his concerns may be alleviated.

speechtext: You know as well as I do, Mr. Hurlburt; there are several different types of blue tongue.

speechtext:
Yes, well that is what I am saying. You could be telling us that the type they had in Europe was altogether a different type than we had in the Okanagan.
MR. Whelan: Which type do you want to know about?

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-NUMBER OF CATTLE AND SHEEP DESTROYED UNDER BLUE TONGUE CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext:
I want to know if the type we had in the Okanagan is the type they had in Europe.
MR. Whelan: I will let Dr. Reid or Dr. McGowan comment.
Dr. Reid said:
Mr. Chairman, we have not as yet recovered any virus from the animals we have slaughtered from the Okanagan Valley. The diagnosis has been based solely on the results of the Kaufmann fixation tests carried out on blood samples collected from the cattle. So we cannot answer your question yet; we have the virus but we have not been able to type it.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-NUMBER OF CATTLE AND SHEEP DESTROYED UNDER BLUE TONGUE CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext:
So what we are saying is that we jumped the gun and we announced an eradication program and went against the B.C. cattlemen's recommendations before we even knew what we had.
Dr. Reid: We do not know the type of virus we have. We know that we have exposure to blue tongue virus based on serological results from tests that have been carried out, and we are confident that they are accurate to the best of our ability.
As I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks, the minister stated, and I quote:
We can make all this available to you. It is not confidential; it is factual.
As of four o'clock this afternoon I had received absolutely no information from the minister's office. However, I found out on my own that 524 head of cattle have been destroyed in British Columbia, that $269,654 has been paid out for herds that have been destroyed, that 49 herds are infected in British Columbia, plus eight deer that are positive reactors.
After talking to my colleague, the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker), I am convinced the following questions are uppermost in the minds of all ranchers in southern British Columbia: what is going to happen to our herds this fall after roundup-isolation, quarantine or eradication? How can we plan if wild game are affected? Why are our armed forces in Europe eating American beef if the disease is so terrible? What enabled the United States to pioneer the Japanese market if the disease is that serious?
In my remarks this evening I have proved that the Minister of Agriculture implemented a program of eradication before he had proof of the most important point: what type of blue tongue do we have? If the type is altogether different and much more serious than the type now prevalent in the United States, the minister has gambled and won. However, if the minister has gambled and lost, we all know who the loser will be; not the Minister of Agriculture but the B.C. rancher.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-NUMBER OF CATTLE AND SHEEP DESTROYED UNDER BLUE TONGUE CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to
Adjournment Debate
respond to the hon. gentlemen this evening and as I begin may I express the regret of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and of his parliamentary secretary for their inability to be present tonight to answer personally.
The hon. member, on May 17, asked how many cattle and sheep have had to be slaughtered under the blue tongue eradication program and how the program related to wild game. Before I answer those questions in detail I would first want to state for the record the minister's firm and well-founded view that Canada has the most disease-free animal population in the world, and we intend to maintain that enviable record.
As of May 17 the numbers were as follows: Cattle; herds tested, 65; positive herds, 49; negative herds, 16; cattle tested, 7,908; positive cattle, 875; negative cattle, 7,033. Sheep; flocks tested, 2; sheep tested, 140 (two sheep were being re-bled as the first samples were unsatisfactory for test); positive sheep, 0; negative sheep, 138. Wild game; deer tested, eight, positive deer, four, (two of which were on the Elkink Ranch); negative deer, four; bighorn sheep tested, four; positive bighorn sheep, zero; negative bighorn sheep, four; mountain goats tested, three; positive mountain goats, zero; negative mountain goats, three.
A permit to shoot 30 deer for testing purposes has been obtained from the provincial authorities. The bighorn sheep and mountain goats are being taken by capture gun and as many as possible will be tested.
At this point there is no indication that blue tongue is widespread in the game in the area and it should be noted that two of the deer which reacted positively were in close association with the heavily infected herd initially uncovered. Deer are not usually any threat to livestock as carriers of the disease. Researchers working in endemic areas have found that blue tongue usually kills deer; any that survive are considered to be immune, non-carriers.
The staff of the Health of Animals Branch is now involved in the process of tracing and testing cattle which have moved from the infected area to other parts of British Columbia. Cattle which moved into Alberta from the infected area have already been slaughtered in the normal course of events with feeder cattle. Movements from the area to Ontario are now being traced and submitted to test.
Officials are now arranging to collect at least 1,000 blood samples from Canadian cattle bordering on the United States in Alberta. This sampling procedure will be extended along the U.S. border into Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Ontario.
It is apparent that the officials of the Health of Animals Branch are making every effort to rid Canada of this foreign disease as soon as possible. With the full co-operation of everyone, hopefully the success of this program will be as great as that which has been evidenced by this country on previous occasions in the complete eradication of foreign animal diseases.
